Active recall

Spot the true one

Every option looks right. Only one is. Each wrong option hides one small slip (a swapped word, a near-miss number, a reversed arrow) that students really make. Read every word before you click: you get one try.

Lesson 1 · What an OS actually does open lesson ↗

Which correctly describes time sharing?

  • The OS runs one program for a short while, then switches to another, so each seems to have its own CPU. Taking turns on the CPU, fast enough that nobody notices, is how one CPU is virtualized into many.
  • The OS gives each program its own CPU core for its whole run, so each seems to have its own CPU. That is splitting in space, and there are far more programs than cores. Time sharing means programs take turns on the same CPU.
  • The OS runs one program until it finishes, then starts another, so each seems to have its own CPU. Running to completion is not sharing. The OS switches after a short while, long before the program finishes.
  • The OS runs one program for a short while, then switches to another, so each seems to have its own memory. Time sharing virtualizes the CPU. A private memory comes from each process's address space.

Which is TRUE about mechanism vs policy?

  • The context switch is a mechanism, answering how; the scheduler is a policy, answering which. Saving one process's registers and loading another's is the how; choosing who runs next is the which.
  • The context switch is a policy, answering which; the scheduler is a mechanism, answering how. Swapped: the context switch is the mechanism and the scheduler is the policy.
  • The context switch is a mechanism, answering which; the scheduler is a policy, answering how. The labels are right but the questions are swapped: a mechanism answers how, a policy answers which.
  • The context switch is a mechanism, answering how; the scheduler is a mechanism, answering when. The scheduler is a policy: it decides which process runs next.

Which correctly describes a process's address space?

  • A private, pretend memory that starts at address 0 and belongs only to that one process. Each process sees its own virtual memory from 0 upward; the OS and hardware translate it to real RAM.
  • A private, pretend memory that starts at address 0 and is shared by every copy of the program. Each process gets its own, even two copies of the same program (that is the mem.c demo).
  • A real, physical region of RAM that starts at address 0 and belongs only to that one process. It is virtual: it starts at 0 only in the process's view, and each address is translated to a different physical one.
  • A private, pretend memory that starts at address 0 and is never translated by the hardware. Every virtual address is translated into a physical address by the OS and hardware.

Two copies of your mem.c run with address randomization turned off. Which is TRUE?

  • Both print the same address for p, and each value climbs by 1 from its own starting number. Same virtual address, but separate address spaces, so each process has its own integer (6, 7… and 8, 9… in the run above).
  • Both print the same address for p, so both values climb together from one shared starting number. The same virtual address does not mean shared memory: each process has its own copy of the integer.
  • Each prints a different address for p, and each value climbs by 1 from its own starting number. With randomization off, both get the same virtual address (0x555555559010 above). Different addresses come from ASLR.
  • Both print the same address for p, and each value climbs by 2 because both processes add 1 to it. Each process adds 1 only to its own integer, so each climbs by 1.

What is the address that lines 16–17 of your mem.c print?

  • A virtual address in that process's own address space, which the hardware translates to a physical one. Programs only ever see virtual addresses; translation to real RAM happens behind their back.
  • A physical RAM address, so two processes that print the same one are sharing that integer. It is virtual. Two processes can print the same one and still use different physical memory.
  • A virtual address that is equal to the physical address whenever randomization is turned off. Turning off ASLR only makes the virtual address repeat. It is still translated.
  • A virtual address in one address space that every process running mem shares. Every process gets its own address space, even two copies of the same program.

Which is TRUE about running your file as ./mem 5?

  • argc is 2, so the check passes; *p starts at 5 and the first value printed is 6. Line 19 sets 5, then the loop sleeps, adds 1 and only then prints: 6 first.
  • argc is 1, so the check fails; the program prints its usage line and exits. argc counts the program name too: ./mem 5 gives 2.
  • argc is 2, so the check passes; *p starts at 5 and the first value printed is 5. Line 22 adds 1 before line 23 prints, so the first value is 6.
  • argc is 2, so the check passes; the first value printed is 6, before the address line. The address is printed once, before the loop (lines 16–17).

Which is TRUE about two threads in the same process?

  • They share the heap and global variables, but each one has its own stack and PC. Threads share the address space (code, heap, globals) and open files; each has its own stack, registers and PC.
  • They share the stack and PC, but each one has its own heap and global variables. Swapped: the heap and globals are shared, the stack and PC are per thread.
  • They share the heap, global variables and stack, but each one has its own PC. Each thread also has its own stack, because each is at a different point in its own function calls.
  • They share nothing in memory, and each one has its own heap, globals, stack and PC. That describes two processes. Threads share the address space (code, heap, globals).

A global int counter is incremented by two threads of one process, and, in a separate run, by two processes running the same program. Which is TRUE?

  • The two threads update one shared counter; the two processes each update their own copy. Threads share globals, so they can race on one counter; processes have separate address spaces.
  • The two threads each update their own copy; the two processes update one shared counter. Swapped: threads share the counter; processes each have their own.
  • The two threads update one shared counter; the two processes update one shared counter too. Two processes have separate address spaces, just like the two copies of mem.c.
  • The two threads each update their own copy; the two processes each update their own copy. Threads share globals; that sharing is exactly what makes the race possible.

Which sequence is right for the machine steps inside counter++?

  • LOAD counter into this thread's register, ADD 1 to that register, STORE the register back to counter. Three separate steps, and memory only changes on the STORE.
  • LOAD counter into this thread's register, STORE the register back to counter, ADD 1 to that register. Wrong order: the ADD comes before the STORE, otherwise the old value is written back.
  • LOAD counter into a register both threads share, ADD 1 to that register, STORE the register back to counter. Each thread has its own registers. Only counter in memory is shared.
  • LOAD counter into this thread's register, ADD 1 to counter in memory, STORE the register back to counter. The ADD changes the register, not memory. counter only changes on the STORE.

counter starts at 4. Threads A and B each run counter++ once: A LOAD → B LOAD → B ADD → A ADD → A STORE → B STORE. Which is TRUE?

  • counter ends at 5: both threads loaded 4, so both store 5. Both registers start from the same old 4, so one increment is lost.
  • counter ends at 6: each thread adds 1, so the two adds give 6. Both ADDs work on a register that holds the old 4, so both produce 5.
  • counter ends at 4: B's STORE overwrites A's STORE with the old value. B stores its register, which holds 5, not the old 4.
  • counter ends at 6: A stores 5, then B loads 5 and stores 6. B loaded before A stored, so B's register holds 4, not 5.

Which is TRUE about a race condition?

  • The result depends on how the threads' steps happen to interleave, so it can differ from run to run. Where a switch lands between a LOAD and its STORE decides how many increments are lost.
  • The result depends on which thread was created first, so it is the same on every run. It depends on the timing of the interleaving, which changes from run to run.
  • The result depends on how the threads' steps happen to interleave, but only on a machine with several CPUs. It happens on one CPU too: a switch between a thread's LOAD and STORE is enough.
  • The result is always exactly half the expected value, because one thread's work is lost. Only some increments are lost, a different number each run (e.g. 18,921,533 instead of 20,000,000).

Which is TRUE about persistence?

  • RAM is volatile and a disk is persistent; the file system is the part of the OS that manages persistent data. RAM forgets everything on power loss; disks and SSDs keep data, and the file system organises it.
  • RAM is persistent and a disk is volatile; the file system is the part of the OS that manages persistent data. Swapped: RAM is volatile and the disk is persistent.
  • RAM is volatile and a disk is persistent; the virtual memory system is the part of the OS that manages persistent data. Address spaces virtualize RAM. Persistent data is managed by the file system.
  • RAM is volatile and a disk is persistent; the file system manages persistent data and assumes no crash mid-write. The file system must stay consistent even if the machine crashes mid-write.

Which correctly matches an OS design goal to its meaning?

  • Protection / isolation: one program can't harm another program or the OS. Isolating processes from one another is the key to protection.
  • Reliability: one program can't harm another program or the OS. Reliability means the OS itself must not crash. Not harming each other is protection / isolation.
  • Protection / isolation: the OS keeps its own time and space overhead low. Low overhead is performance.
  • Abstraction: one program can't harm another program or the OS. Abstraction means making the hardware easy to use (processes, address spaces, files).

Lesson 2 · The process open lesson ↗

Which is TRUE about programs and processes?

  • A process is a running program; one program on disk can be running as several processes at once. Run ./a.out twice and there is one program file but two processes, each with its own state.
  • A process is a running program; one program on disk can be running as only one process at a time. Run it twice and you get two processes from one program.
  • A process is a program stored on disk; it becomes a program once the OS loads and starts it. Swapped: the program is on disk; it becomes a process when it runs.
  • A process is a running program; it holds the program's code and data but not its registers or open files. A process's state also includes its registers and its open files.

Which is TRUE about the program counter (PC)?

  • It holds the address of the next instruction to run, and is also called the instruction pointer. The CPU fetches from the address in the PC; x86 calls it eip, the instruction pointer.
  • It holds the address of the instruction that just finished, and is also called the instruction pointer. It holds the next instruction to fetch and execute.
  • It holds the address of the top of the stack, and is also called the instruction pointer. The top of the stack is the stack pointer's job.
  • It holds the address of the next instruction to run, and is also called the frame pointer. Its other name is the instruction pointer. The frame pointer marks the current function's stack frame.

Which is TRUE about the stack pointer (SP) and the stack?

  • SP points to the top of the stack, which holds function parameters, local variables and return addresses. The stack tracks function calls, and SP marks where its top currently is.
  • SP points to the top of the stack, which holds function parameters, local variables and malloc()'d blocks. malloc() memory comes from the heap, not the stack.
  • SP points to the next instruction to run, and the stack holds parameters, local variables and return addresses. The next instruction is the PC. SP points to the top of the stack.
  • SP points to the top of the stack, which holds the program's code, static data and return addresses. Code and static data are loaded into their own region. The stack holds parameters, locals and return addresses.

Which list is a process's machine state (OSTEP)?

  • Its memory (code, static data, heap, stack), its registers (PC, SP, …), and its I/O information (open files). These three are everything the process can read or change, so they are what the OS saves and restores.
  • Its memory (heap and stack only), its registers (PC, SP, …), and its I/O information (open files). Memory is the whole address space: code and static data too.
  • Its memory (code, static data, heap, stack), its PC only, and its I/O information (open files). All the registers are part of it (PC, SP, frame pointer, general-purpose).
  • Its memory (code, static data, heap, stack), its registers (PC, SP, …), and its program file on disk. The file on disk is the program. The third part is I/O information: the files it has open.

Which is TRUE about the process API calls (both OSTEP and Dr. Bilal's slide list these)?

  • Destroy forcefully halts a runaway process, and Status reports info such as how long it has run. Destroy = "halt a runaway process"; Status = "get some status info" (how long it has run, what state it is in).
  • Destroy forcefully halts a runaway process, and Status suspends it so it can be resumed later. Suspend/resume is OSTEP's misc. control. Status only reports info (run time, state).
  • Wait forcefully halts a runaway process, and Status reports info such as how long it has run. Halting a runaway process is Destroy. Wait waits for a process to stop running.
  • Destroy frees the entry of a process that has already exited, and Status reports info such as how long it has run. Destroy stops a process that is still running (a runaway) forcefully. Cleaning up after an exit is not Destroy's job.

Which is TRUE about Dr. Bilal's restaurant analogy for the process API?

  • The menu and the waiter are both the API; the kitchen is the OS, which does the real work. Menu = what you can ask for, waiter = carries the request and the response (both API), kitchen = the OS.
  • The menu is the API and the waiter is the OS; the kitchen is the hardware, which does the real work. The waiter is the API too (the messenger), and the kitchen is the OS.
  • The menu and the waiter are both the API; the kitchen is the user program, which does the real work. The kitchen is the OS: it has the data and does the complex work. The program is the customer ordering.
  • The menu and the kitchen are both the API; the waiter is the OS, which carries the request. Swapped: the waiter is the API (the messenger) and the kitchen is the OS.

Which is TRUE about the three file descriptors every UNIX process starts with?

  • 0 is standard input, 1 is standard output, 2 is standard error. They are already open, so a program can read the keyboard and print without opening anything.
  • 0 is standard output, 1 is standard input, 2 is standard error. Swapped: 0 is input and 1 is output.
  • 1 is standard input, 2 is standard output, 3 is standard error. Numbering starts at 0: 0, 1, 2.
  • 0 is standard input, 1 is standard error, 2 is standard output. 1 is standard output and 2 is standard error.

Which is TRUE about how the OS sets up a new process's memory?

  • It fills the stack with argc and argv, and gives it a small heap that grows with malloc(). Arguments to main() go on the stack; dynamic memory comes from the heap.
  • It fills the heap with argc and argv, and gives it a small stack that grows with malloc(). Swapped: argc/argv go on the stack, and malloc() uses the heap.
  • It fills the stack with argc and argv, and gives it a fixed heap that malloc() can never grow. The heap starts small and grows as the program asks for more.
  • It fills the stack with argc and argv, and places the heap right next to the stack with no gap. There is a free gap between heap and stack so both can grow toward each other.

Your monster runs with MAX_FILES = 50 and nothing else open. Which is TRUE?

  • The opens return 3 through 52, because 0, 1 and 2 are already open. 50 numbers starting at 3 end at 52, as in your output.
  • The opens return 0 through 49, because the monster opens 50 files. 0, 1 and 2 are already open (stdin, stdout, stderr), so the first free number is 3.
  • The opens return 3 through 53, because 0, 1 and 2 are already open. Off by one: 50 numbers from 3 are 3 to 52.
  • The opens return 1 through 50, because descriptor 0 is reserved for errors. Numbering starts at 0, and 0 is standard input; errors go to 2.

In the monster, open() fails when i = 7 and the loop breaks. Which is TRUE about the cleanup loop?

  • fds[7] is −1 and skipped, but fds[8] to fds[49] were never set, so close() may get garbage. Only the failing slot was written; the rest still hold whatever was on the stack.
  • fds[7] to fds[49] are all −1 and skipped, so only fds[0] to fds[6] are closed. Only fds[7] got −1. Slots 8 to 49 were never assigned.
  • fds[7] is −1, so close(-1) runs and the program crashes before the other slots. The if (fds[i] >= 0) check skips −1; the problem is the unset slots after it.
  • fds[7] is −1 and skipped, and the cleanup loop stops there, so slots 8 to 49 are never touched. The cleanup loop has no break; it visits all 50 slots, including the garbage ones.

Each successful open() in the monster grows which part of the process's machine state?

  • Its I/O information: the list of files the process has open. Open files are the third part of machine state, next to memory and registers.
  • Its registers: each open file is held in a CPU register until it is closed. The descriptor number is just an int; the open file is recorded in the process's I/O information.
  • Its heap: each open file is a block that open() allocates with malloc(). open() is a system call; the OS records the file in the process's open-file list, not in your heap.
  • Its code: each open file is loaded into the code region until it is closed. Opening a file doesn't load it as code; it adds an entry to the open-file list.

Which correctly describes the Ready state?

  • The process could run right now, but the OS has chosen not to run it at this moment. It is waiting only for the scheduler, not for any event.
  • The process can't run right now, because it is waiting for an I/O request to finish. Waiting for I/O is Blocked.
  • The process could run right now, and the OS must run it next because it has been waiting. The scheduler decides; being Ready gives no guarantee of running next.
  • The process could run right now, but it has given up the CPU until some event happens. Waiting for an event is Blocked. In Ready, it is the OS that chose not to run it.

Which correctly describes the Blocked state?

  • The process started an I/O request and can't continue until it is done; meanwhile another process can use the CPU. Blocking frees the CPU for someone else, which is the whole point of the state.
  • The process started an I/O request and can't continue until it is done; meanwhile the CPU must stay idle. The OS runs another process meanwhile, so the CPU stays busy.
  • The OS took the CPU away because its time slice ran out, and it waits to be scheduled again. That is being descheduled: Running → Ready, not Blocked.
  • The process started an I/O request and, as soon as it is done, goes straight back to Running. When the I/O is done it goes to Ready and waits for the scheduler.

Which transition really exists in the Running / Ready / Blocked diagram?

  • Blocked → Ready, when the I/O the process was waiting for is done. "I/O: done" puts it back in the Ready queue; the scheduler picks it later.
  • Blocked → Running, when the I/O the process was waiting for is done. There is no such arrow: it must go to Ready first.
  • Ready → Blocked, when the process starts an I/O request while waiting. A Ready process isn't running, so it can't start I/O. Only Running → Blocked exists.
  • Running → Ready, when the process starts an I/O request. Starting I/O is Running → Blocked. Running → Ready is the OS descheduling it.

Which correctly maps xv6 states?

  • SLEEPING = Blocked, RUNNABLE = Ready, UNUSED = a free process-table slot. Sleeping waits for an event, runnable waits for the CPU, and unused means no process is in that slot.
  • SLEEPING = Ready, RUNNABLE = Blocked, UNUSED = a free process-table slot. Swapped: SLEEPING is Blocked and RUNNABLE is Ready.
  • SLEEPING = Blocked, RUNNABLE = Running, UNUSED = a free process-table slot. RUNNABLE = Ready (waiting for the CPU). Running has its own state, RUNNING.
  • SLEEPING = Blocked, RUNNABLE = Ready, UNUSED = a process still being created. A process still being set up is EMBRYO.

Which is TRUE about a zombie process?

  • It has exited, but its parent hasn't called wait() yet, so its entry stays to hold the exit status. The entry lingers until the parent reaps it with wait().
  • It has exited, and its parent has already called wait(), so its entry stays to hold the exit status. wait() reaps it; a zombie is one that has not yet been waited for.
  • Its parent has exited, but it is still running, so its entry stays until init collects it. That is an orphan. A zombie has itself exited.

Which is TRUE about the Process Control Block (PCB)?

  • It is a C struct kept for each process in the process list; xv6 saves the process's registers in its context field. One PCB per process, holding identity, state, saved registers, memory info and open files.
  • It is one C struct shared by all processes in the process list; xv6 saves the registers in its context field. There is one PCB per process: each entry in the process list is a PCB.
  • It is a C struct kept for each process in the process list; xv6 saves the process's registers in its chan field. chan is what a sleeping process waits on. Registers go in context.
  • It is a C struct kept for each process in the process list; it holds the saved registers but not the PID or state. It holds the PID, state and parent too, alongside registers, memory info and open files.

In your process_manager.c, which is TRUE about is_active?

  • is_active == 0 means the slot is free, like xv6's UNUSED; create takes the first such slot. Line 54 picks the first slot with !is_active, just as a new process needs a free (UNUSED) entry.
  • is_active == 0 means the process has exited but not been reaped, like xv6's ZOMBIE. terminate frees the slot at once; no parent has to collect anything. That is UNUSED.
  • is_active == 0 means the process is still being set up, like xv6's EMBRYO. create fills the fields and sets is_active = 1 in one go; 0 means no process in the slot.
  • is_active == 1 means the slot is free, like xv6's UNUSED; create takes the first such slot. Reversed: 1 means a process is using the slot, 0 means free.

next_address is 100 when you type create 7 40 60 20. Which is TRUE about what map then shows for PID 7?

  • heap: [140-199] and stack: [200-219], and next_address becomes 220. Code is 100–139 (40 bytes), heap starts right after at 140, stack at 200; 100 + 120 = 220.
  • heap: [140-200] and stack: [200-220], and next_address becomes 220. print_segment prints base + limit − 1 as the end: 60 bytes from 140 end at 199.
  • heap: [141-200] and stack: [201-220], and next_address becomes 221. Each segment starts exactly at the previous base + size (line 72), with no gap byte.
  • heap: [140-199] and stack: [200-219], and next_address stays 100. Line 77 adds the total (120) to next_address.

You type terminate 5 for a running PID 5. Which is TRUE?

  • Its slot can be reused at once, but its memory is not given back, because next_address never goes down. Line 89 only clears is_active; nothing touches next_address.
  • Its slot can be reused at once, and its memory is given back, because next_address goes down. No line lowers next_address; the memory is never reused.
  • Its memory can be reused at once, but its slot is not given back, because is_active stays 1. Reversed: line 89 sets is_active = 0, freeing the slot; the memory is what stays lost.
  • Its slot stays taken until a parent collects it, because terminated processes become zombies. This program has no parents and no wait(); the slot is free immediately.

Two threads run inside one process. Which is TRUE?

  • They share the heap, globals and open files, but each has its own PC, registers and stack. One address space and one set of open files per process; each thread is its own stream of execution, so it needs its own PC, registers and stack.
  • They share the heap, globals and stack, but each has its own PC and registers. Each thread has its own stack: it calls its own functions, with its own locals and return addresses.
  • They share the heap and globals, but each has its own PC, registers, stack and open files. Open files belong to the process, so the threads share them.
  • They share the code and globals, but each has its own heap, PC, registers and stack. The heap is part of the process's address space, so it is shared (that is why threads can pass malloc()'d data to each other).

Why can two threads race on a global counter, while a parent and its fork()ed child each doing counter++ cannot?

  • The threads share one address space, so both update the same counter; each process updates its own copy. fork() gives the child its own copy of the address space, so there is no shared variable to race on.
  • The threads share one stack, so both update the same counter; each process updates its own copy. Each thread has its own stack, and a global isn't on the stack anyway. What they share is the address space (globals, heap).
  • The threads share one set of registers, so both update the same counter; each process updates its own copy. Registers are per thread (each has its own A_reg/B_reg in the trace). The race is on the shared memory value.
  • The threads share one address space, so both update the same counter; the processes never run interleaved. Processes are interleaved too (time sharing). They don't race because each has its own copy of counter.

Lesson 3 · fork, exec and wait open lesson ↗

Which is TRUE about system calls in C?

  • They always run in kernel mode, and fork() and getpid() come from <unistd.h>. System calls do privileged work; <unistd.h> is the POSIX header for the process calls.
  • They always run in user mode, and fork() and getpid() come from <unistd.h>. System calls run in kernel (privileged) mode.
  • They always run in kernel mode, and fork() and getpid() come from <sys/wait.h>. <sys/wait.h> gives wait()/waitpid(). fork and getpid are in <unistd.h>.
  • They run in kernel mode only when they touch a device, and fork() comes from <unistd.h>. They always run in kernel mode, whatever they do.

int rc = fork(); Which is TRUE about the value of rc?

  • In the child it is 0; in the parent it is the child's PID; −1 means no child was created. 0 tells the child who it is; the parent needs the child's PID (for wait/waitpid).
  • In the parent it is 0; in the child it is the child's PID; −1 means no child was created. Swapped: the child gets 0 and the parent gets the child's PID.
  • In the child it is 0; in the parent it is the parent's own PID; −1 means no child was created. The parent gets the child's PID, so it knows which child it made.
  • In the child it is 0; in the parent it is the child's PID; −1 means the child was created but crashed. −1 means the fork failed and no child exists at all.

Which is TRUE about where a newly forked child begins?

  • It starts just after the fork() call, with its own copy of the parent's variables. It was copied at the moment of the fork, so it continues from there with its own address space.
  • It starts at the top of main(), with its own copy of the parent's variables. It does not restart main(); it continues right after the fork.
  • It starts just after the fork() call, sharing the parent's variables with it. It gets its own copy: a change in one process doesn't show up in the other.
  • It starts just after the fork() call, with all variables reset to their starting values. The copy keeps the current values the parent had at the fork.
Printed to a terminal, which output is possible?
printf("A\n");
int rc = fork();
if (rc == 0) printf("B\n");
else         printf("C\n");
  • A C B: A prints once, then the parent and child print in either order. Without wait() the scheduler decides who runs first, so the parent's C may come before the child's B.
  • A B A C: A prints in both processes, then each prints its own letter. A printed before the fork, when the child didn't exist yet, so it prints once.
  • B A C: the child prints first, then the parent prints A and C. A is printed before the fork, so it must come first.
  • A B: A prints once, then only the child prints its letter. The parent also continues after the fork and prints C.

Your Task 1 run printed the parent's line (PID 15230) before the child's (PID 15231). Which is TRUE?

  • return_child was 15231 in the parent and 0 in the child; the parent's line came first only by chance. After the fork the scheduler decides who runs first; nothing in Task 1 forces an order.
  • return_child was 15231 in the parent and 0 in the child; the parent's line always comes first. Not always: with no wait() the child can run first on another run.
  • return_child was 15230 in the parent and 0 in the child; the parent's line came first only by chance. The parent gets the child's PID (15231), not its own.
  • return_child was 0 in the parent and 15231 in the child; the parent's line came first only by chance. Swapped: the child gets 0, the parent gets 15231.

In Task 2 the child sleeps 1 s and the parent sleeps 2 s. Which is TRUE?

  • The child is Blocked for 1 s and usually prints first, but sleep() doesn't guarantee the order. A sleeping process waits for an event (the time to pass): Blocked. Only wait() guarantees an order.
  • The child is Ready for 1 s and usually prints first, but sleep() doesn't guarantee the order. A sleeping process can't run, so it is Blocked (xv6 SLEEPING), not Ready.
  • The child is Blocked for 1 s and always prints first, because sleep() guarantees the order like wait(). sleep() only biases timing. Your own comment says it: "not a real guarantee".
  • The parent is Running for 2 s and prints last, because sleeping keeps it on the CPU. Sleeping gives up the CPU: the parent is Blocked for those 2 s.

During Task 3, ps lists PIDs 15600 and 15601, both p2a. Which is TRUE?

  • They are two separate processes running one program; 15601 was made by 15600's fork(). One program file, two processes, each with its own PID and address space.
  • They are one process listed twice; fork() only added a second branch inside it. fork() makes a real new process; that's why ps shows two PIDs.
  • They are two separate processes running one program; 15600 was made by 15601's fork(). 15600 printed "Hello Students" and forked; it is the parent, 15601 is the child.
  • They are two separate processes running one program; both are in the Running state while they sleep. A sleeping process is Blocked, not Running.

Every process runs fork(); fork(); fork(); in a row. Which is TRUE?

  • 8 processes exist at the end, 7 of them new. Each fork doubles the count: 23 = 8, minus the original = 7 new.
  • 8 processes exist at the end, 8 of them new. The original isn't new: 2n − 1 = 7 new.
  • 4 processes exist at the end, 3 of them new. Each fork is run by every process alive, so the count doubles each time: 8.
  • 7 processes exist at the end, 6 of them new. 7 is the number of new ones; the total is 23 = 8.

Which is TRUE about if (fork() == 0) fork();?

  • 3 processes: P0's child forks again, so the chain is P0 → P1 → P2 and P2 is P0's grandchild. Only the child gets 0 and enters the if, so the child is the one that forks.
  • 3 processes: P0 forks again, so P1 and P2 are both P0's children (siblings). P0 gets a positive value and skips the if; only the child forks again.
  • 4 processes: every process runs both forks, so there are 22 = 4. The second fork is inside the if, so only one process runs it: 3.
  • 3 processes: P1 forks again, so P1 and P2 are siblings, both children of P0. Whoever calls fork() is the parent: P2 is P1's child, P0's grandchild.
Printed to a terminal, how many lines does this print?
for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
    printf("x\n");
    fork();
}
  • 3 lines: 1 process prints in the first iteration, 2 processes in the second. Here the printf runs before that iteration's fork, so the last fork's children print nothing.
  • 6 lines: 2 processes print in the first iteration, 4 processes in the second. That is the count when printf comes after the fork. Here it comes before.
  • 4 lines: 4 processes exist at the end, and each one prints once. The 2 children made by the last fork leave the loop without printing: 1 + 2 = 3.
  • 2 lines: only the original process runs the loop's printf. Children continue the loop from just after the fork, so the first child prints too.

Which is TRUE about int wc = wait(NULL); in a parent?

  • The parent blocks until one of its children finishes, and wc is that child's PID. wait() returns the PID of the child it reaped.
  • The parent blocks until one of its children finishes, and wc is 0. 0 is what fork() returns in the child. wait() returns the child's PID.
  • The parent blocks until any process on the system finishes, and wc is that process's PID. It only waits for its own children; with none it returns −1 at once.
  • The parent blocks until all of its children finish, and wc is the number of children. One wait() returns after one child finishes, with that child's PID.

Your Task 4 output ends with parent of 15801 (wc:15801). Which is TRUE?

  • wc is 15801 because wait() returns the PID of the child it reaped. The parent's only child, 15801, exited; wait() returned its PID.
  • wc is 15801 because wait() returns the same value fork() returned in the child. fork() returned 0 in the child. wait() returns the reaped child's PID.
  • wc is 15801 because wait() returns the PID of the newest process on the system. wait() only deals with the caller's own children.
  • wc is 15801 because wait() returns the caller's own PID plus one. The PIDs just happen to be consecutive; wait() returns the child's PID.

Task 6's parent calls waitpid on child 1, then child 2, then child 3. Child 3 finishes first. Which is TRUE?

  • The parent stays blocked in the first waitpid until child 1 exits; child 3 stays a zombie until its own waitpid. waitpid(pid, …) waits for that child only; an exited child waits as a zombie until it is reaped.
  • The first waitpid returns child 3's PID at once, because child 3 finished first. That is what wait(NULL) would do. waitpid(return_child, …) waits for child 1.
  • The parent stays blocked in the first waitpid until child 1 exits; child 3 is removed by the OS at once. An exited child stays as a zombie until its parent reaps it.
  • The parent prints its final line as soon as child 3 exits, then waits for the other two. The printf comes after all three waitpid calls.

Why does your Task 5 program make exactly 3 children and no grandchildren?

  • Each later fork() sits in the parent's else branch, so only the original process reaches it. Children get 0 and take the if branch, which contains no fork.
  • Each later fork() sits in the child's if branch, so only the newest child reaches it. Then each child would fork the next one: a chain of grandchildren. The forks are in the else.
  • Each child calls wait() before the next fork(), so the children can't reach it. Task 5 has no wait() at all; the else nesting keeps children away from the forks.
  • Each child's exit(0) is the only thing that stops it reaching the later fork() calls. Without exit(0) a child still skips the else and returns: still 3 children (tested).

Which is TRUE about fork() and exec()?

  • fork() makes a process with a new PID; a successful exec() keeps the same PID and never returns. exec() replaces the program inside the existing process, so there is nothing to return to.
  • fork() makes a process with a new PID; a successful exec() also gives the process a new PID. exec() creates no process: the PID stays the same.
  • fork() makes a process with a new PID; a successful exec() keeps the same PID and returns 0. A successful exec() never returns; if it returns, it failed.
  • fork() keeps the caller's PID for the child; a successful exec() gives a new PID and never returns. Swapped: fork() gives a new PID, exec() keeps the same one.

A child calls execvp("ls", args) and it succeeds. Which is TRUE?

  • Its code, static data, heap and stack are replaced, but its PID and open file descriptors stay. Keeping the open descriptors is what lets a shell redirect output before the exec.
  • Its code and static data are replaced, but its old heap and stack are kept for the new program. The heap and stack are re-initialized too; nothing of the old program remains.
  • Its code, static data, heap and stack are replaced, and all its open file descriptors are closed. Open descriptors stay open, otherwise ls > out.txt could not work.
  • Its code, static data, heap and stack are copied into a new process, and the old program keeps running. exec() creates no new process; the old program is gone.

Which is TRUE about your Task 7 run?

  • ls -l ran as PID 18036, the child's own PID, and the "exec failed" line never ran. exec replaces the program inside the same process and doesn't return on success.
  • ls -l ran as a new PID made by execvp, and the "exec failed" line never ran. exec creates no new process: ls kept PID 18036.
  • ls -l ran as PID 18035, the parent's PID, and the "exec failed" line never ran. Only the child (18036) called execvp; the parent was waiting.
  • ls -l ran as PID 18036, the child's own PID, and the "exec failed" line ran after ls ended. After a successful exec that line no longer exists in the process, so it never runs.

You run Task 8 as ./exec pid exec.c. Which is TRUE?

  • argc is 3; myargs[1] gets argv[1] ("pid") and myargs[3] is NULL. argv[0] is "./exec", so the two user words are argv[1] and argv[2].
  • argc is 2; myargs[1] gets argv[1] ("pid") and myargs[3] is NULL. argc counts the program name too: 3. Line 1 of task8_exec.c checks argc != 3.
  • argc is 3; myargs[0] gets argv[0] ("./exec") and myargs[3] is NULL. myargs[0] is the new program's name, "grep".
  • argc is 3; myargs[1] gets argv[1] ("pid") and myargs needs no NULL at the end. execvp finds the end of the list by the NULL; without it, it reads past the array.

Which is TRUE about final.c when all four exec calls succeed?

  • 5 processes exist: only the parent reaches each fork(), since every child becomes another program. A successful exec never returns, so no child ever gets to the next fork().
  • 16 processes exist: every process reaches each later fork(), so 4 forks give 24. 2n needs every process to run every fork. Here each child execs away first.
  • 5 processes exist, and they run one at a time, because the parent waits right after each fork(). The waitpid calls are all after the four forks, so the children run at the same time.
  • 5 processes exist, but the four children share one PID, because exec keeps the PID. exec keeps each child's own PID; each fork() made a different one (21119–21122).

A child with fds 0, 1 and 2 open runs close(1); then open("out.txt", O_CREAT | O_WRONLY | O_TRUNC, 0644);. Which is TRUE?

  • open() returns 1, because it takes the lowest free descriptor, so standard output now goes to the file. fd 1 was just freed, so the file becomes fd 1, and anything written to stdout lands in it.
  • open() returns 3, because it takes the next unused number, so standard output still goes to the screen. open() takes the lowest free descriptor, which is 1.
  • open() returns 1, because it takes the lowest free descriptor, so standard error now goes to the file. fd 1 is standard output; standard error is fd 2.
  • open() returns 0, because it takes the lowest descriptor, so standard input now comes from the file. fd 0 is still open, so it isn't free. The lowest free one is 1.

Which sequence is right for a shell running ls -l > out.txt?

  • Shell forks → child redirects stdout to the file → child execs ls → shell waits. The redirection must happen in the child, after the fork and before the exec.
  • Shell forks → child execs ls → child redirects stdout to the file → shell waits. After a successful exec the child's own code is gone, so it must redirect before exec.
  • Shell forks → shell redirects stdout to the file → child execs ls → shell waits. The child redirects; the shell's own descriptors are separate after the fork and must stay on the screen.
  • Shell forks → child redirects stdout to the file → shell execs ls → child waits. Roles swapped: the child execs and the shell (parent) waits.

Which is TRUE about int main(int argc, char *argv[])?

  • argc counts the program name too, and every argv entry is a string, even "5". ./sumto 5 → argc = 2, argv[1] = "5", which needs atoi to become the int 5.
  • argc doesn't count the program name, and every argv entry is a string, even "5". It does count it: argv[0] is the program name, so ./sumto 5 has argc = 2.
  • argc counts the program name too, and a number like 5 arrives in argv as an int. Every entry is a string (char *). Use atoi(argv[1]) to get the int.
  • argc counts the program name too, and the program name is stored in argv[1]. The name is argv[0]; the first real argument is argv[1].

In the lesson's Makefile, run: all is followed by the lines ./sumto 5 and ./countlines notes.txt. Which is TRUE about make run?

  • It first brings all up to date, recompiling any program whose .c changed, then runs both programs. run depends on all, so make builds the dependencies first, then runs run's commands.
  • It first runs both programs, then brings all up to date, recompiling any program whose .c changed. Reversed: dependencies are built before the target's own commands run.
  • It runs both programs without compiling anything, because run is not the first target. "First target" only decides what a plain make builds. run: all still builds all first.
  • It first recompiles every .c file from scratch, changed or not, then runs both programs. make only rebuilds a target whose dependencies changed since it was last built.

Lesson 4 · Limited direct execution open lesson ↗

Which is TRUE about the order of steps in plain direct execution?

  • The OS sets up the stack with argc/argv before it executes call main(). Steps 1–5 (entry, memory, load, stack, clear registers) all come before step 6, call main().
  • The OS executes call main() before it loads the program into memory. The program must be in memory first: load is step 3, call main() is step 6.
  • The program frees its own memory after it executes return from main(). Wrong actor: the OS frees the process's memory (step 9) and removes it from the process list (step 10).
  • The OS creates the process-list entry after main() returns. Creating the entry is step 1, the very first thing. After the return, the OS removes the entry.

Direct execution has two problems. Which is TRUE about how limited direct execution fixes them?

  • Restricted operations: user/kernel modes plus system calls. Running forever: the timer interrupt. Modes stop a program doing raw I/O itself (it must trap to the OS); the timer lets the OS take the CPU back.
  • Restricted operations: the timer interrupt. Running forever: user/kernel modes plus system calls. Swapped. Modes handle restricted operations; the timer handles a program that never gives up the CPU.
  • Restricted operations: user/kernel modes plus system calls. Running forever: the yield() system call. yield() is the cooperative approach, which trusts the process. An infinite loop never yields: the timer interrupt is needed.
  • Restricted operations: the OS checks every instruction in software. Running forever: the timer interrupt. That would throw away direct execution's speed. The hardware enforces it with user/kernel modes.

Which is TRUE about user mode and kernel mode?

  • User mode runs ordinary instructions only; kernel mode can run anything, including I/O and privileged instructions. Applications run in user mode and the OS runs in kernel mode with full access.
  • User mode can run ordinary instructions and I/O; kernel mode can run anything, including privileged instructions. User mode can't do I/O either: that's why programs need system calls.
  • User mode runs ordinary instructions only; kernel mode can run privileged instructions only. Kernel mode can run anything, ordinary instructions included.
  • User mode runs ordinary instructions only; a program enters kernel mode by setting the mode bit itself. Changing the mode is privileged. A program can only get there through a trap.

A program in user mode executes a privileged instruction. Which is TRUE?

  • The CPU raises an exception, control passes to the OS, and the OS will likely kill the program. The hardware refuses and hands control to the OS, which decides what to do (usually terminate).
  • The CPU quietly skips the instruction, and the program carries on with the next one. The CPU raises an exception; it doesn't silently ignore it.
  • The CPU switches to kernel mode and runs the instruction for the program, then returns. That would defeat the protection. The CPU raises an exception and the OS handles it.
  • The CPU raises an exception, and the hardware itself kills the program without the OS. The hardware passes control to the OS, and the OS decides to kill it.

Which is TRUE about the mode bit?

  • The CPU holds the current mode in a mode bit; a trap sets it to kernel and return-from-trap sets it to user. It flips up on the trap and back down on the return-from-trap.
  • The OS holds the current mode in the PCB; a trap sets it to kernel and return-from-trap sets it to user. The mode is kept by the CPU (hardware), in the mode bit.
  • The CPU holds the current mode in a mode bit; a trap sets it to user and return-from-trap sets it to kernel. Swapped: a trap raises privilege to kernel; return-from-trap lowers it to user.
  • The CPU holds the current mode in a mode bit; a user program can set it to kernel with an ordinary instruction. Only a trap can raise the privilege level; otherwise protection would be meaningless.

Which is TRUE about what happens when a program executes a trap?

  • The hardware saves the registers onto the kernel stack, switches to kernel mode, and jumps to the handler in the trap table. Save, raise privilege, jump: all three are done by the hardware, using addresses the OS set at boot.
  • The hardware saves the registers onto the user stack, switches to kernel mode, and jumps to the handler in the trap table. They go onto the process's kernel stack.
  • The OS saves the registers onto the kernel stack, switches to kernel mode, and jumps to the handler in the trap table. The OS isn't running yet at that moment: the hardware does all three.
  • The hardware saves the registers onto the kernel stack, stays in user mode, and jumps to the handler in the trap table. A trap raises the privilege to kernel mode; the handler runs as the kernel.

Which is TRUE about the trap table?

  • The OS installs it at boot with a privileged instruction; a user program only supplies a system-call number. The OS decides in advance where each event and system-call number leads.
  • Each program installs its own at startup with a system call; a user program only supplies a system-call number. Only the OS, at boot, installs it. A program that could install one could take over the machine.
  • The OS installs it at boot with an ordinary instruction; a user program only supplies a system-call number. Installing the trap table is a privileged instruction.
  • The OS installs it at boot with a privileged instruction; a user program supplies the handler's address. The program gives only a number; letting it choose an address would let it skip permission checks.

Trace line 34 reads write(3, "PID: 25848 \t UID: 1000 \n", 24) = 24. Which is TRUE?

  • The program trapped into the kernel, which wrote 24 bytes to log.txt (descriptor 3) and returned 24. Descriptor 3 is the file openat returned on line 33; the value after = is the byte count.
  • The program trapped into the kernel, which wrote 24 bytes to the screen (descriptor 3) and returned 24. The screen is descriptor 1; descriptor 3 is log.txt.
  • The C library wrote 24 bytes to log.txt itself in user mode, then told the kernel it was done. User mode can't do I/O. Writing the file needs a trap into the kernel.
  • The program trapped into the kernel, which wrote 24 bytes to log.txt and returned descriptor 24. write returns the number of bytes written, not a descriptor.

While trace line 37's read(0, …) waits for you to type, which is TRUE?

  • The process is Blocked inside the kernel, and the OS can run other processes until input arrives. It trapped in for the read and can't continue until the keyboard event happens.
  • The process is Running in user mode, checking again and again whether a key has been pressed. It is waiting inside the kernel in the Blocked state, not spinning in user mode.
  • The process is Ready inside the kernel, and the OS can run other processes until input arrives. Waiting for an event is Blocked. Ready would mean it could run right now.
  • The process is Blocked inside the kernel, and the CPU stays idle until input arrives. Blocking frees the CPU: the OS runs other processes meanwhile.

Line 26 of sys_writer.c writes "Log written to file.\n" with length 22. Which is TRUE?

  • The text is 21 bytes, so the 22nd byte written is the string's ending '\0', as trace line 35 shows. The trace prints "Log written to file.\n\0", 22: the NUL went to the screen too.
  • The text is 22 bytes, so length 22 writes exactly the message and nothing more. Count it: "Log written to file." is 20 characters, plus \n = 21.
  • The text is 21 bytes, so write() stops at the '\0' and only 21 bytes are written. write() doesn't look for a '\0'; it writes exactly the length given: 22 (trace line 35).
  • The text is 21 bytes, so the 22nd byte is read from past the end of memory and the program crashes. A string literal has a hidden '\0' at the end, so byte 22 exists; it is written, nothing crashes.

Which is TRUE about return-from-trap?

  • The hardware restores the registers from the kernel stack, switches to user mode, and jumps to the program's PC. It is the mirror image of the trap: restore, lower privilege, jump back.
  • The hardware restores the registers from proc_t, switches to user mode, and jumps to the program's PC. It restores from the kernel stack. proc_t is used by the OS's switch().
  • The hardware restores the registers from the kernel stack, switches to kernel mode, and jumps to the program's PC. Return-from-trap lowers privilege to user mode.
  • The hardware restores the registers from the kernel stack, switches to user mode, and jumps to main() again. It jumps to the saved PC, just after the trap. Only the very first start lands on main().

In the LDE protocol, how does the OS start a user process for the very first time?

  • It fills the kernel stack with registers and PC, then executes return-from-trap, as if returning from a system call. Reusing return-from-trap gets the switch to user mode and the jump to main() in one step.
  • It fills the kernel stack with registers and PC, then executes a trap, as if the process made a system call. A trap goes into the kernel. To leave it and start the program, the OS uses return-from-trap.
  • It fills the user stack with registers and PC, then executes return-from-trap, as if returning from a system call. Return-from-trap restores from the kernel stack; the user stack gets argc/argv.
  • It calls main() like a normal function, and the program runs in kernel mode until it exits. Then there would be no limits. The program must run in user mode, entered via return-from-trap.

Which is TRUE about the cooperative approach?

  • The OS regains the CPU only on a system call (including yield()) or an illegal operation; a loop with no system calls means a reboot. With no timer, a process that never traps never gives the OS a chance to run.
  • The OS regains the CPU on a system call, an illegal operation or a timer interrupt; a loop with no system calls gets preempted. The timer interrupt is the non-cooperative approach; cooperative has no timer.
  • The OS regains the CPU only on a system call (including yield()); an illegal operation is simply ignored. An illegal operation (divide by zero, bad memory) traps into the OS, which also gives it control.
  • The OS regains the CPU only on a system call or an illegal operation; a loop with no system calls is killed by the OS after a while. The OS never runs again, so it can't kill anything: the only fix is to reboot.

Which is TRUE about the timer interrupt?

  • The OS starts the timer at boot with a privileged instruction; when it fires, the OS's handler runs and the scheduler may keep the same process. The timer only guarantees the OS gets control back; whether to switch is the scheduler's choice.
  • The OS starts the timer at boot with an ordinary instruction; when it fires, the OS's handler runs and the scheduler may keep the same process. Starting the timer is privileged, otherwise a program could switch it off.
  • The OS starts the timer at boot with a privileged instruction; when it fires, the OS's handler runs and must switch to another process. The scheduler may keep running the same process; a switch isn't required.
  • The OS starts the timer at boot with a privileged instruction; when it fires, a busy process can ignore it and keep running. The interrupt can't be ignored by the process; it halts it and runs the OS's handler.

Which is TRUE about the context switch?

  • The OS saves the old process's registers, restores the new one's, and switches to the new process's kernel stack. Switching kernel stacks makes the next return-from-trap land in the new process.
  • The hardware saves the old process's registers, restores the new one's, and switches to the new process's kernel stack. The context switch is OS code (switch()), run after the scheduler decides to switch.
  • The OS saves the old process's registers, restores the new one's, and keeps using the old process's kernel stack. It must switch kernel stacks, or return-from-trap would resume the old process.
  • The OS saves the old process's registers, restores the new one's, and does this on every timer interrupt, even if the scheduler keeps the same process. The context switch runs only when the scheduler picks a different process; otherwise return-from-trap simply resumes the same one.

A timer interrupt leads to a switch from A to B. Which correctly describes the two register saves for A?

  • The hardware saves A's user registers onto A's kernel stack; the OS saves A's kernel registers into proc_t(A). Implicit save by hardware on the interrupt, then explicit save by switch().
  • The hardware saves A's user registers into proc_t(A); the OS saves A's kernel registers onto A's kernel stack. Places swapped: hardware uses the kernel stack, the OS uses proc_t.
  • The OS saves A's user registers onto A's kernel stack; the hardware saves A's kernel registers into proc_t(A). Actors swapped: the hardware does the first save, the OS the second.
  • The hardware saves A's user registers onto A's user stack; the OS saves A's kernel registers into proc_t(A). The hardware saves them onto A's kernel stack.

Which is TRUE about the kernel stack?

  • Each process has its own kernel stack, where the hardware saves its user registers on every trap or interrupt. One per process, which is why switching to B's kernel stack makes the CPU return into B.
  • All processes share one kernel stack, where the hardware saves their user registers on every trap or interrupt. Each process has its own kernel stack.
  • Each process has its own kernel stack, kept in user memory, where the hardware saves its user registers on every trap or interrupt. The kernel stack lives in kernel memory; if the program could reach it, it could forge its saved registers before return-from-trap.
  • Each process has its own kernel stack, where the hardware saves its user registers only during a context switch. The hardware saves them there on every trap or interrupt, switch or not.

A timer interrupt arrives while the OS is already handling another interrupt. Which is TRUE?

  • The OS can disable interrupts while it handles one, but if it keeps them off too long, interrupts can be lost. OSTEP: disabling interrupts during interrupt processing means no other one is delivered, but doing it for too long "could lead to lost interrupts".
  • The OS can disable interrupts while it handles one, and it can keep them off as long as it likes at no cost. Not free: keep them off too long and interrupts get lost.
  • The user program can disable interrupts while the OS handles one, but if it keeps them off too long, interrupts can be lost. Wrong actor: turning interrupts off is privileged, so only the OS (in kernel mode) can do it.
  • The OS can disable interrupts while it handles one, and on multi-core CPUs that alone protects all kernel data. Multi-core is exactly where the OS also needs locks to protect its internal data structures.

Which is TRUE about the locks the OS uses inside the kernel?

  • They protect the kernel's internal data structures when several things run in the kernel at once, especially on multi-core CPUs. Several activities can be in the kernel at the same time; locks stop them corrupting shared kernel data.
  • They protect each user program's private variables when several things run in the kernel at once, especially on multi-core CPUs. They protect the kernel's internal data structures, not a program's own variables.
  • They protect the kernel's internal data structures when several things run in the kernel at once, especially on single-core CPUs. The slides and OSTEP single out multi-core CPUs (multiprocessors), where kernel code really runs in parallel.
  • They protect the kernel's internal data structures when several things run in the kernel at once, and are simple and bug-free. OSTEP warns the opposite: locking "can be complicated and lead to a variety of interesting and hard-to-find bugs".

Lesson 5 · Scheduling basics: FIFO, SJF, STCF, RR open lesson ↗

Which is TRUE about relaxing the workload assumptions (in words, so the numbering doesn't matter)?

  • Relaxing "all jobs arrive at the same time" breaks SJF, so we invent STCF. A long job that arrives first can't be stopped by non-preemptive SJF, so STCF adds preemption.
  • Relaxing "all jobs arrive at the same time" breaks FIFO, so we invent SJF. That is the "same length" assumption: FIFO's convoy effect led to SJF.
  • Relaxing "the run-time is known" breaks SJF, so we invent STCF. STCF needs run-times too. Unknown run-times lead to MLFQ.
  • Relaxing "all jobs arrive at the same time" breaks STCF, so we invent Round Robin. RR came from a new metric (response time), not from a relaxed assumption. Late arrivals broke SJF, fixed by STCF.

Which is TRUE about the assumption "the run-time of each job is known"?

  • SJF and STCF both depend on it; a real OS doesn't know run-times, which is why MLFQ learns from the past. Both must compare job lengths (SJF by burst, STCF by time left), so both need an oracle.
  • SJF and RR both depend on it; a real OS doesn't know run-times, which is why MLFQ learns from the past. RR just cycles with a fixed slice and needs no run-times. The two that need them are SJF and STCF.
  • SJF depends on it but STCF doesn't; a real OS doesn't know run-times, which is why MLFQ learns from the past. STCF compares remaining times, so it needs the run-times as well.
  • SJF and STCF both depend on it; a real OS reads run-times from the program file, so MLFQ isn't needed. No such field exists: the OS has no oracle, so MLFQ predicts from past behaviour.

Which is TRUE about turnaround time?

  • Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time. It measures the whole stay, from arriving to being completely done: Tturnaround = Tcompletion − Tarrival.
  • Turnaround time = first-run time − arrival time. That is response time. Turnaround ends at completion, not at the first run.
  • Turnaround time = completion time − first-run time. It starts counting at arrival, not at the first run: time spent waiting before the first run counts too.
  • Turnaround time = completion time − burst time. You subtract the arrival time, not the job's length (burst).

A job arrives at t = 4, first gets the CPU at t = 9, and completes at t = 17. Which is TRUE?

  • Its response time is 5. Response = first run − arrival = 9 − 4 = 5.
  • Its response time is 9. You forgot to subtract the arrival: 9 − 4 = 5.
  • Its response time is 13. 17 − 4 = 13 is its turnaround time. Response uses the first run: 9 − 4 = 5.
  • Its response time is 8. 17 − 9 = 8 is the time from first run to completion, which is neither metric. Response = 9 − 4 = 5.

Which is TRUE about the convoy effect?

  • Under FIFO, short jobs queue behind one long job, so average turnaround is poor. Same total work, but the long job in front pushes every short job's completion time late. That is the convoy.
  • Under SJF, long jobs queue behind many short jobs, so average turnaround is poor. Reversed. Running short jobs first is how SJF cures the convoy. The victims are short jobs stuck behind a long one under FIFO.
  • Under RR, short jobs queue behind one long job, so average turnaround is poor. RR gives every job a slice in turn, so no job waits for a long one to finish. The convoy is a FIFO problem.
  • Under FIFO, the CPU idles while one job waits for I/O, so turnaround is poor. That is the I/O overlap problem. The convoy effect is short jobs stuck behind a long job.

FIFO. A arrives at t = 0 (burst 5), B at t = 2 (burst 3), C at t = 4 (burst 2). Which is TRUE?

  • Average turnaround is 17/3 ≈ 5.67. A 0–5, B 5–8, C 8–10. Turnaround: (5 − 0) + (8 − 2) + (10 − 4) = 5 + 6 + 6 = 17, so 17/3 ≈ 5.67.
  • Average turnaround is 23/3 ≈ 7.67. That averages the completion times (5 + 8 + 10) and forgets to subtract the arrivals: (5 + 6 + 6)/3 = 17/3 ≈ 5.67.
  • Average turnaround is 10/3 ≈ 3.33. That averages the bursts (5 + 3 + 2). Turnaround = completion − arrival: (5 + 6 + 6)/3 = 17/3 ≈ 5.67.
  • Average turnaround is 7/3 ≈ 2.33. That is the average response time, (0 + 3 + 4)/3. Turnaround = (5 + 6 + 6)/3 = 17/3 ≈ 5.67.

Which is TRUE about SJF?

  • SJF is non-preemptive: once a job starts, it runs to completion even if a shorter job arrives. SJF only makes a decision when the running job finishes. Adding preemption turns it into STCF.
  • SJF is preemptive: when a shorter job arrives, it takes the CPU from the running job. That is STCF (preemptive SJF). Plain SJF is non-preemptive.
  • SJF is non-preemptive: once a job starts it runs to completion, and no run-times need to be known. SJF must know every run-time to find the shortest job (an oracle). That is why MLFQ was invented.
  • SJF re-decides at every arrival, comparing the remaining time of every job. That is STCF. SJF decides only when the running job finishes.

Which is TRUE about SJF and average turnaround?

  • When all jobs arrive together, SJF gives the lowest possible average turnaround. OSTEP: SJF is provably optimal for average turnaround if all jobs arrive at the same time.
  • When all jobs arrive together, SJF gives the lowest possible average response time. RR beats it on response (three 5-s jobs: SJF 5 s, RR with a 1-s slice 1 s). SJF's guarantee is about turnaround.
  • Even when jobs arrive at different times, SJF gives the lowest possible average turnaround. A long job that arrives first blocks later short ones and the convoy returns. With staggered arrivals, STCF is the optimal one.
  • When all jobs arrive together, SJF and FIFO always give the same average turnaround. Only if FIFO's order happens to be shortest-first. A 12, B 3, C 3 in that order: FIFO gives 15 s, SJF gives 9 s.

Which line correctly computes response time in scheduler.c?

  • jobs[i].start_time - jobs[i].arrival Response = first run − arrival, and start_time is the first run.
  • jobs[i].completion_time - jobs[i].arrival That is turnaround (line 25). Response ends at the first run: start_time.
  • jobs[i].completion_time - jobs[i].start_time That is just how long the job ran once started, which is neither metric. Subtract the arrival.
  • jobs[i].start_time - jobs[i].length You subtract the arrival, not the job's length.

simulate_fifo gets A (length 4), B (length 7), C (length 2), all arriving at 0, in that order. After the clock loop, which is TRUE about C?

  • C's start_time is 11 and its completion_time is 13. The clock goes 0 → 4 (A) → 11 (B), so C starts at 11 and ends at 13.
  • C's start_time is 0 and its completion_time is 2. That is the SJF order. simulate_fifo does not sort, so C waits behind A and B.
  • C's start_time is 13 and its completion_time is 15. 13 is when C completes, not when it starts. Line 17 records the clock before line 18 adds C's length: start = 11, completion = 11 + 2 = 13.
  • C's start_time is 11 and its completion_time is 2. Line 19 stores the clock (current_time) after adding the length, not the length itself: 11 + 2 = 13.

You run your unchanged simulate_fifo on A (arrives 0, length 2) and B (arrives 5, length 3). Which is TRUE about the line it prints for B?

  • Job B: Turnaround = 0, Response = -3 The loop ignores arrivals, so B "starts" at 2 and completes at 5: 5 − 5 = 0 and 2 − 5 = −3. (Checked by running a copy.)
  • Job B: Turnaround = 3, Response = 0 That is the correct answer on paper (B waits until 5, runs 5–8). The code never waits for the arrival, so it prints 0 and −3.
  • Job B: Turnaround = 5, Response = 2 Those are B's raw completion and start times. The code does subtract the arrival (5): 0 and −3.
  • Job B: Turnaround = 0, Response = 3 Sign slip: start (2) − arrival (5) = −3. A negative response is the giveaway that arrivals are ignored.

STCF. A arrives at t = 0 (burst 6). B arrives at t = 3 (burst 4). Which is TRUE at t = 3?

  • A keeps running, because its 3 remaining units are less than B's 4. STCF compares remaining times: A has 6 − 3 = 3 left and B needs 4, so A finishes at 6 and B runs 6–10.
  • B preempts A, because B's burst of 4 is less than A's burst of 6. STCF compares remaining time, not original bursts. A has only 6 − 3 = 3 left, so it keeps the CPU.
  • B preempts A, because under STCF a newly arrived job always runs first. A newcomer runs only if it needs less time than the running job has left. Here 4 > 3, so A continues.
  • A keeps running, because STCF never preempts a job once it has started. Right outcome, wrong reason. STCF does preempt (that is what it adds to SJF); here it doesn't need to, since 3 < 4.

Which change would turn simulate_stcf into non-preemptive SJF?

  • Only run the pick loop when the last job has finished (or nothing has run yet). SJF decides only when the running job finishes. Skipping the pick at other ticks means nobody can take over mid-run.
  • Change < to <= on line 22. That only changes who wins a tie. The pick still runs every tick, so it is still preemptive.
  • Compare length instead of remaining on line 22. The pick still runs every tick, so a job can still be thrown off mid-run. It just compares the wrong number.
  • Remove the arrival check jobs[i].arrival <= current_time. Then jobs from the future could be picked before they exist. That breaks it; it doesn't make it SJF.

P (arrives 0, length 5) is listed before Q (arrives 0, length 5). Which is TRUE about what simulate_stcf does?

  • P runs 0–5, then Q runs 5–10. Tie at t = 0 → strict < keeps the first listed (P). After one tick P has 4 left, less than Q's 5, so P never loses the CPU. (Checked by running a copy.)
  • Q runs 0–5, then P runs 5–10. Q would win the tie only with <= (the last equal job wins). With <, P wins.
  • P and Q swap every tick, like RR with a 1-tick slice. Once P runs one tick it has 4 left against Q's 5, so it is strictly shorter and keeps going.
  • P runs 0–1, then Q preempts it and runs 1–6. Q would need less remaining time than P's 4 to preempt. 5 is not less than 4.

A (burst 4) arrives at 0, B (burst 6) at 1, C (burst 3) at 2. The CPU ran A 0–4 | B 4–10 | C 10–13. Of FIFO, SJF and STCF, which could have produced this chart?

  • FIFO only. At t = 4 both B and C wait. FIFO picks B (arrived first). SJF and STCF would pick C (3 < 6). (RR with a slice of 6 or more would also give this chart, since it then never cuts a job short.)
  • FIFO and SJF only. SJF picks the shortest waiting job at t = 4: C (3), not B (6).
  • FIFO, SJF and STCF. SJF and STCF both pick C at t = 4 (3 < 6), so the chart would show C 4–7, B 7–13.
  • SJF and STCF only. Running B before C is arrival order, which is FIFO; shortest-first would run C first.

A (burst 4) arrives at 0, B (burst 5) at 1, C (burst 1) at 2. The CPU ran A 0–4 | C 4–5 | B 5–10. Of FIFO, SJF and STCF, which could have produced this chart?

  • SJF only. At t = 4 SJF picks C (1) over B (5). STCF would have preempted A at t = 2 (C's 1 < A's 2 left), and FIFO would run B before C.
  • SJF and STCF only. At t = 2, C needs 1 and A has 4 − 2 = 2 left, so STCF preempts: A 0–2, C 2–3, A 3–5, B 5–10.
  • FIFO and SJF only. FIFO runs in arrival order: B (arrived at 1) before C (arrived at 2). Here C ran first.
  • FIFO, SJF and STCF. An unsplit chart can still rule STCF out: at t = 2, C (1) < A's 2 left, so STCF would have preempted. FIFO is out too (C ran before B).

Four jobs of 3 s each all arrive at t = 0 and run under SJF. Which is TRUE?

  • The average response time is 4.5 s. They start at 0, 3, 6, 9 → (0 + 3 + 6 + 9)/4 = 18/4 = 4.5.
  • The average response time is 7.5 s. That is the average turnaround, (3 + 6 + 9 + 12)/4. Response uses the first-run times: 18/4 = 4.5.
  • The average response time is 9 s. 9 s is only the last job's response. Average: (0 + 3 + 6 + 9)/4 = 4.5.
  • The average response time is 1.5 s. That is RR with a 1-s slice: (0 + 1 + 2 + 3)/4. SJF runs them back to back: 4.5.

Which is TRUE about response time?

  • It is first-run time − arrival time, and STCF is not particularly good at it. STCF runs short jobs to completion first, so jobs that arrive together wait a long time for their first turn.
  • It is completion time − arrival time, and STCF is not particularly good at it. Completion − arrival is turnaround. Response ends at the first run.
  • It is first-run time − arrival time, and STCF is the optimal policy for it. STCF is optimal for turnaround. For response it is poor; RR is the response-time policy.
  • It is first-run time − arrival time, and it matters most on batch systems with no users waiting. It arose with time-shared machines, where users sit at terminals waiting for the system to respond.

Which is TRUE about the Round Robin time slice?

  • The time slice must be a multiple of the timer-interrupt period. The OS only gets control back when the timer fires, so a slice can only end on a timer tick (10 ms timer → 10, 20, 30 ms, …).
  • The timer-interrupt period must be a multiple of the time slice. Swapped. The slice is a multiple of the timer period.
  • The time slice must be shorter than the timer-interrupt period. The OS can only switch when the timer fires, so the slice can't end between ticks. It is a whole multiple of the period.
  • The time slice can be any length, because RR doesn't rely on the timer interrupt. RR depends on the timer to take the CPU back (Lesson 4), so the slice must be a multiple of the timer period.

Which is TRUE about the trade-off between the policies?

  • RR optimises response time but hurts turnaround; SJF/STCF optimise turnaround but hurt response. That is the fundamental trade-off: neither kind of policy wins on both metrics.
  • RR optimises turnaround but hurts response; SJF/STCF optimise response but hurt turnaround. Swapped. RR is the response-time policy; SJF/STCF are the turnaround policies.
  • RR optimises both response and turnaround; only its context-switch cost holds it back. RR stretches every job out, so its turnaround is among the worst (three 4-s jobs: RR(1) 11 s vs SJF 8 s).
  • STCF optimises both turnaround and response, because it always runs the shortest job. Jobs that arrive together still wait their turn: three 4-s jobs → STCF response (0 + 4 + 8)/3 = 4 s vs RR's 1 s.

Three jobs of 6 s each arrive at t = 0. Round Robin with a 2-s slice. Which is TRUE?

  • Average response is 2 s and average turnaround is 16 s. First runs at 0, 2, 4 → 6/3 = 2. The third round ends A at 14, B at 16, C at 18 → 48/3 = 16.
  • Average response is 2 s and average turnaround is 12 s. 12 is SJF's turnaround, (6 + 12 + 18)/3. Under RR the jobs finish at 14, 16, 18 → 16.
  • Average response is 6 s and average turnaround is 16 s. 6 is SJF's response, (0 + 6 + 12)/3. Under RR they first run at 0, 2, 4 → 2.
  • Average response is 2 s and average turnaround is 18 s. 18 is when the last job finishes. The average is (14 + 16 + 18)/3 = 16.

Which is TRUE about amortizing the context-switch cost in RR?

  • A longer slice amortizes the switch cost: the same fixed cost is paid less often. With a 1 ms switch, a 10 ms slice wastes about 10% and a 100 ms slice under 1%. The price is worse response time.
  • A shorter slice amortizes the switch cost: each switch becomes cheaper. The cost of one switch doesn't depend on the slice. Amortizing means paying it less often, which needs a longer slice.
  • A longer slice amortizes the switch cost, and it also improves response time. A longer slice makes response time worse (RR drifts towards FIFO). That is the trade-off.
  • A longer slice amortizes the switch cost by making each switch faster. Each switch costs the same; it just happens less often.

A running job issues an I/O request. Which is TRUE?

  • It becomes blocked, the scheduler runs another job, and when the I/O completes an interrupt moves it back to ready. Bilal's slide: blocked while waiting, another job gets the CPU, then interrupt → blocked to ready.
  • It becomes blocked, the scheduler runs another job, and when the I/O completes an interrupt moves it straight back to running. There is no Blocked → Running arrow. It goes to ready and waits for the scheduler.
  • It becomes ready, the scheduler runs another job, and when the I/O completes an interrupt moves it back to running. A job waiting for I/O can't use the CPU, so it is blocked, not ready.
  • It becomes blocked, the CPU waits idle until the I/O completes, and then an interrupt moves it back to ready. Idling wastes the CPU. The scheduler should run another job during the I/O.

A needs 15 ms of CPU: it runs 5 ms, does a 5 ms I/O, and repeats (three CPU bursts, two I/Os). B needs 20 ms of CPU and does no I/O. Compare running A completely first and then B, with overlapping (STCF treating each 5 ms burst of A as a job). Which is TRUE?

  • Without overlap all work is done at 45 ms; with overlap, at 35 ms. No overlap: 15 CPU + 10 idle + 20 = 45. Overlap: A 0–5, B 5–10, A 10–15, B 15–20, A 20–25, B 25–35. The CPU never idles, so 15 + 20 = 35.
  • Without overlap all work is done at 45 ms; with overlap, at 25 ms. 25 ms is when A finishes. B still has 10 ms left: it runs 25–35, so everything is done at 35.
  • Without overlap all work is done at 35 ms; with overlap, at 25 ms. Without overlap the CPU idles during A's two I/Os: 15 + 10 + 20 = 45. With overlap: 35.
  • Without overlap all work is done at 50 ms; with overlap, at 35 ms. A does only two I/Os (between its three bursts): 15 + 2 × 5 + 20 = 45.

All jobs arrive at t = 0. Which is the correct core of the SJF pseudocode?

  • Sort by burst ascending; then for each job: start = time, time += burst, finish = time. Record the start before the clock moves, run the whole burst (no preemption), then record the finish.
  • Sort by burst descending; then for each job: start = time, time += burst, finish = time. Shortest first means ascending. Descending runs the longest job first, the worst order.
  • Sort by burst ascending; then for each job: time += burst, start = time, finish = time. Wrong order: start must be recorded before adding the burst, or every job's start equals its finish.
  • Sort by arrival ascending; then for each job: start = time, time += burst, finish = time. Sorting by arrival is FIFO. SJF sorts by burst.

SJF with different arrival times. Which is TRUE about the general loop?

  • Each time the CPU is free, pick the shortest job that has already arrived; if none has, jump the clock to the next arrival. Only arrived jobs can run; if none is waiting, the CPU idles until the next arrival.
  • Each time the CPU is free, pick the shortest unfinished job, even if it hasn't arrived yet. A job can't run before it arrives. Pick from jobs with arrival ≤ time.
  • Each time a new job arrives, pick the shortest job that has already arrived, preempting the running job if needed. Deciding at every arrival with preemption is STCF. SJF decides only when the CPU is free.
  • Each time the CPU is free, pick the shortest job that has already arrived; if none has, end the loop. Jobs may still be on their way. Jump the clock to the earliest unfinished arrival and continue.

Which is TRUE about preemption?

  • STCF and RR are preemptive; FIFO and SJF run each job to completion. STCF preempts when a shorter job arrives; RR preempts when the slice ends. FIFO and SJF never take the CPU away.
  • SJF and RR are preemptive; FIFO and STCF run each job to completion. SJF and STCF are swapped: STCF is preemptive SJF, and plain SJF is non-preemptive.
  • Only RR is preemptive; FIFO, SJF and STCF run each job to completion. STCF is preemptive too: it switches whenever a newcomer needs less than the running job has left.
  • SJF, STCF and RR are preemptive; only FIFO runs each job to completion. SJF is non-preemptive: once a job starts, it runs to completion.

Lesson 6 · MLFQ: a scheduler that learns open lesson ↗

Which is TRUE about what MLFQ is trying to do?

  • Optimise turnaround like SJF and minimise response time like RR, without knowing job lengths in advance. Both goals at once, learning each job's nature from its past behaviour.
  • Optimise turnaround like RR and minimise response time like SJF, without knowing job lengths in advance. Swapped: SJF is the turnaround policy and RR the response-time policy.
  • Optimise turnaround like SJF and minimise response time like RR, using each job's length given in advance. The whole point: the OS doesn't know job lengths, so MLFQ learns them.
  • Optimise turnaround like SJF and minimise response time like RR, by giving each job a fixed priority. MLFQ varies a job's priority based on its observed behaviour (OSTEP); a fixed priority couldn't learn anything.

Why do MLFQ's two goals clash?
