  • SJF can't be used because job lengths are unknown, and RR improves response time but hurts turnaround. Exactly Dr. Bilal's two "challenge" lines.
  • SJF can't be used because job lengths are unknown, and RR improves turnaround but hurts response time. Reversed: RR improves response and hurts turnaround.
  • SJF can't be used because it is preemptive, and RR improves response time but hurts turnaround. SJF is non-preemptive. The obstacle is that job lengths are unknown.
  • SJF can't be used because job lengths are unknown, and RR improves both response time and turnaround. If RR improved both, there would be no clash. It hurts turnaround by stretching every job out.

Which is TRUE about MLFQ's queues?

  • A ready job is on exactly one queue, and the scheduler runs a job from the highest-priority non-empty queue. Each queue is one priority level; Rule 1 says the higher queue always wins.
  • A ready job is on every queue at or below its priority, and the scheduler runs a job from the highest-priority non-empty queue. A ready job is on exactly one queue at a time.
  • A ready job is on exactly one queue, and the scheduler gives every non-empty queue one slice in turn. Queues don't take turns. A lower queue runs only when every higher queue is empty.
  • A ready job is on exactly one queue, and the scheduler runs whichever job has waited longest, on any queue. Waiting time doesn't decide it: priority does (highest non-empty queue first).

A and B are on the top queue, C on the middle queue, D on the bottom queue. All four stay ready, nobody moves between queues, and there is no boost. Which is TRUE?

  • A and B take turns in RR; C runs only when the top queue is empty; D runs only when both higher queues are empty. Rule 2 within a level, Rule 1 between levels.
  • A runs to completion before B; C runs only when the top queue is empty; D runs only when both higher queues are empty. Jobs on the same queue share in RR (Rule 2), not one after another.
  • A and B take turns in RR; C and D take turns in RR whenever the top queue is empty. C and D have different priorities, so C runs first; D waits until C's queue is empty too.
  • A and B take turns in RR; C runs only when the top queue is empty; D gets a slice every few rounds so it doesn't starve. Nothing gives D a turn while higher jobs stay ready. That is starvation. The fix is the priority boost (Rule 5), coming later in this lesson; the question says there is no boost.

Which is TRUE about MLFQ Rule 1?

  • If Priority(A) > Priority(B), A runs and B doesn't. A lower queue gets the CPU only when every higher queue is empty.
  • If Priority(A) > Priority(B), A and B run in RR. RR is Rule 2, for equal priority. Higher priority simply wins.
  • If Priority(A) > Priority(B), B runs whenever A's time slice ends. When A's slice ends, A (or another job at its level) runs again. B waits until no higher-priority job is ready.
  • If Priority(A) > Priority(B), A runs, unless B has less work left. MLFQ doesn't know how much work is left. It picks by priority only.

Which is TRUE about MLFQ Rule 2?

  • If Priority(A) = Priority(B), A & B run in RR. Jobs on the same queue take turns, one time slice each.
  • If Priority(A) = Priority(B), they run FIFO, each to completion. Same-queue jobs share in round robin, one slice each.
  • If Priority(A) = Priority(B), the one with less time left runs first. That is STCF, which needs run-times MLFQ doesn't know. Equal priority → RR.

Which is TRUE about where MLFQ puts a new job?

  • A new job is placed at the highest priority (the top queue). Rule 3: every job gets the benefit of the doubt, as if it might be short.
  • A new job is placed at the lowest priority and moves up if it proves interactive. Rule 3 puts it at the top. MLFQ has no rule that promotes a job level by level.
  • A new job is placed in the queue that matches its expected run-time. MLFQ never knows run-times; every new job starts at the top.
  • A new job is placed in the middle queue until its behaviour is known. Rule 3: highest priority, the top queue.

Which is TRUE about MLFQ's final Rule 4?

  • Once a job's total time at a level reaches its allotment, it moves down one queue. Its time at the level is added up across all its stints; when the total reaches the allotment, its priority is reduced by one level.
  • Once a job uses up its time allotment at a level, it drops straight to the bottom queue. It moves down one queue at a time (Q2 → Q1 → Q0), as in the slides' single long-running job example.
  • A job moves down only if it uses a whole time slice in one go without giving up the CPU. That was old Rule 4a, which could be gamed. Rule 4 adds up all its time at the level.
  • A job's used allotment resets to zero each time it gives up the CPU for I/O. That reset is exactly what the rewrite removed: time counts in total, "regardless of how many times it has given up the CPU".

Which is TRUE about MLFQ Rule 5?

  • After some time period S, all jobs move to the topmost queue and can sink again later. The boost is a fresh start, not a permanent pass: Rule 4 still applies afterwards.
  • After some time period S, all jobs move to the topmost queue and stay there until they finish. The classic diagram mistake. After the boost a CPU-bound job uses one slice per level and walks down again.
  • After some time period S, only the jobs in the bottom queue move up one level. Rule 5 moves all jobs, and all the way to the topmost queue.
  • After some time period S, all jobs move down one queue to make room for new jobs. Reversed: the boost moves everyone up to the top.

How does MLFQ approximate SJF? Which is TRUE?

  • Every job starts at the top, so a short job finishes before it sinks. Long jobs keep using whole slices and sink; short ones are done while still at high priority, so they effectively run first, like SJF.
  • Every job states its run-time on entry, and MLFQ runs the shortest first. MLFQ is never told run-times; it learns them from how the job behaves.
  • Every job starts at the bottom, so long jobs never delay short ones. Rule 3 puts new jobs at the top.
  • Every queue is sorted by remaining time, so the shortest job runs first. Inside a queue, jobs run in RR (Rule 2). MLFQ doesn't know remaining times.

Which is TRUE about starvation in first-attempt MLFQ?

  • Too many interactive jobs hog the top queues, so long jobs starve; the Rule 5 boost fixes it. Every S, the boost lifts the starving long jobs to the top, where they share the CPU in RR.
  • Too many interactive jobs hog the top queues, so long jobs starve; the rewritten Rule 4 fixes it. Rule 4 fixes gaming. Starvation is fixed by the Rule 5 boost.
  • Long jobs hog the top queues, so interactive jobs starve; the Rule 5 boost fixes it. Reversed. Long jobs sink to the bottom; it is the long-running jobs that starve.
  • Too many interactive jobs hog the top queues, so long jobs starve; Rule 3 fixes it. Rule 3 only places new jobs at the top. The fix is the Rule 5 boost.

Which is TRUE about gaming the scheduler?

  • A job does I/O just before its slice ends, so old Rule 4b keeps it on top; the rewritten Rule 4 fixes it. Rule 4 counts the job's total time at the level, so its small pieces add up and it moves down.
  • A job does I/O just before its slice ends, so old Rule 4b keeps it on top; the Rule 5 boost fixes it. The boost lifts everyone, the gamer included. The fix is Rule 4's better accounting.
  • A job does I/O just before its slice ends, so old Rule 4a demotes it unfairly; Rule 4 fixes it. The gamer escapes demotion: it never uses a whole slice, so 4a never fires and 4b keeps it on top.
  • A job does I/O just before its slice ends, so old Rule 4b keeps it on top; Rule 4 fixes it by resetting the allotment after each I/O. Resetting was the bug. Rule 4 accumulates the time instead.

A CPU-bound job sank to the bottom queue, then turned interactive. Which is TRUE?

  • The Rule 5 boost gives it a fresh start at the top, where its new behaviour lets it stay high. This is the "changing behaviour" problem, and the priority boost is its fix.
  • Rule 4b moves it up a level each time it gives up the CPU early. 4b only keeps a job at its same level. Nothing but the boost (Rule 5) moves jobs up.
  • Rule 3 moves it back to the top, because it now behaves like a new job. Rule 3 applies only when a job enters the system. The fix is the Rule 5 boost.
  • It stays at the bottom for good, because MLFQ has no way to notice the change. That was the problem with the first attempt. Rule 5 (the boost) fixes it.

The allotment at the top level is 10 ms. A job runs 4 ms, does a quick I/O, and repeats. Under the rewritten Rule 4, which is TRUE?

  • It moves down during its 3rd run, when its total at the level reaches 10 ms. 4 + 4 = 8 ms after two runs; 2 ms into the third run the total hits 10 ms, so it is demoted.
  • It moves down after its 2nd run, once its total reaches 8 ms. 4 + 4 = 8 < 10, still under the allotment. It drops during the 3rd run, when the total reaches 10.
  • It never moves down, because it always gives up the CPU before its slice ends. That was true under old Rule 4b. Rule 4 adds the pieces up: 4 + 4 + 2 = 10 → demoted in the 3rd run.

In your run, which is TRUE about what turning the boost on (period 30) changed?

  • Job 3 finished at 243 instead of 275; its first run stayed at t = 13. The boost lifts a demoted job back up, so it finishes sooner. It can't make the first run happen any earlier.
  • Job 3 finished at 243 instead of 275; its first run moved earlier than t = 13. Both runs print "first ran at t=13". A boost only helps a job that has already been demoted.
  • Job 4 finished at 253 instead of 285; Job 3 was unchanged. It is the other way round: Job 4 finished at 285 both times, and Job 3 moved from 275 to 243.
  • Both long jobs finished 32 ticks earlier with the boost on. Only Job 3 gained 32 ticks. Job 4 finished at 285 in both runs.

Which line in hunger.c puts a brand-new job at the highest priority (Rule 3)?

  • Line 26: Job newcomer = {total_jobs + 1, now, 4, 4, 0, QUANTUM, 0, 0}; The fifth field is current_queue, set to 0, and queue 0 is the top here.
  • Line 26, because its fourth field (4) is the top queue's number. The fourth field is remaining_time (4). The queue is the fifth field: 0.
  • Line 51: if (!job_list[i].done) job_list[i].current_queue = 0; That is the boost (Rule 5), for jobs already in the system. New jobs get queue 0 on line 26.
  • Line 76: job_list[pick].current_queue++; That is demotion (Rule 4), moving a job down.

Which is TRUE about time slices in a tuned MLFQ?

  • High-priority queues get short slices; low-priority queues get long slices. Top queues hold interactive jobs that need only a brief turn (good response); bottom queues hold CPU-bound jobs, where long slices mean fewer switches. E.g. 10 / 20 / 40 ms.
  • High-priority queues get long slices; low-priority queues get short slices. Swapped. Short slices at the top, long slices at the bottom.
  • Every queue gets the same slice, because Rule 2 runs each queue in RR. Rule 2 says nothing about slice length. Tuned MLFQs vary it, e.g. 10 / 20 / 40 ms, and Solaris goes from 20 ms to a few hundred ms.
  • High-priority queues get short slices so that long CPU-bound jobs finish sooner. Right layout, wrong reason. Short top slices keep interactive jobs responsive; CPU-bound jobs live in the low queues with long slices.

MLFQ: top slice 2, middle slice 4, bottom FCFS, no boost. A (burst 6), B (burst 3), C (burst 2) all arrive at t = 0 in that order. Which is TRUE?

  • The average turnaround time is 9. Top: A 0–2, B 2–4, C 4–6 (done). Middle: A 6–10 (done), B 10–11 (done). Turnaround (10 + 11 + 6)/3 = 27/3 = 9.
  • The average turnaround time is 8. That runs B before A in the middle queue (B 6–7, A 7–11 → 24/3). Inside a queue, jobs run in the order they arrived there: A dropped first. Answer 9.
  • The average turnaround time is 11. 11 is when the last job (B) finishes. Average: (10 + 11 + 6)/3 = 9.
  • The average turnaround time is 2. That is the average response time, (0 + 2 + 4)/3. Turnaround uses completion: 9.

Same trace (slices 2 / 4 / FCFS; A 6, B 3, C 2, all at t = 0). Which is TRUE?

  • C's burst ends at t = 6, exactly when its top slice does, so it finishes and never moves down. A job that finishes at the end of its slice simply leaves the system.
  • C uses its whole top slice from 4 to 6, so it drops to the middle queue and finishes there. C needed only 2, so it is finished at 6. A finished job doesn't move down.
  • B runs before A in the middle queue, because B has less work left than A. MLFQ doesn't know remaining work. Inside a queue it is RR in arrival order there: A (dropped at 2) before B (dropped at 4).
  • A uses its full middle slice from 6 to 10, so it drops to the bottom queue before finishing. A had exactly 6 − 2 = 4 left, so it finishes at 10. The bottom queue is never used here.

Which line in run_mlfq is Rule 3 (a new job starts at the highest priority)?

  • jobs[i].current_queue = 0; In mlfq.c queue 0 is the top (the first one the pick loop scans), so every job starts there.
  • jobs[i].current_queue = Q_LEVELS - 1; That is Dr. Bilal's numbering (highest number on top). In this code, queue Q_LEVELS − 1 = 2 is the bottom.
  • jobs[i].current_queue = 1; The printout calls the top column "Q1", but the array index of the top queue is 0.
  • jobs[i].current_queue = Q_LEVELS; Index 3 is past the end of a 3-level array (valid indexes are 0–2). The top is 0.

MLFQ2 (quanta2 = {3, 6, 12}). A job has just used up its allotment in the middle queue. Which is TRUE right after lines 166–171?

  • It is in queue 2 with allot_left = 12. next_q = 1 + 1 = 2, and line 170 sets allot_left = quanta[2] = 12.
  • It is in queue 2 with allot_left = 6. 6 is the allotment of the level it just left. Line 170 uses quanta[next_q] = 12.
  • It is in queue 0 with allot_left = 3. That is what a boost does (Rule 5). Running out of allotment moves it down, to queue 2.
  • It is in queue 1 with allot_left = 12. It moves down a level: next_q = current_queue + 1 = 2.

After a 1-tick turn, Job 3 is sent to the back of its queue by the Rule 2 branch (line 178). Which is TRUE about its allot_left?

  • It stays where it is and keeps counting down on later turns. Only demotion (line 170) and the boost refill it. Counting total time at a level is the rewritten Rule 4.
  • It is refilled to quanta of its current queue. That is per-turn counting (the old 4a/4b idea), which lets a job game the scheduler. The Rule 2 branch never touches allot_left.
  • It is refilled to quanta[0]. Apart from the start (line 71), only the boost (lines 89 and 97) sets quanta[0]. The Rule 2 branch doesn't change it.
  • It is set to 0, so the job drops a level on its next turn. Nothing sets it to 0. It drops only once its own count reaches 0 (line 165).

Lesson 7 · Lottery and stride: sharing by tickets open lesson ↗

Which is TRUE about a proportional-share (fair-share) scheduler?

  • It tries to guarantee each job a certain percentage of CPU time. A job's share is its tickets divided by the total (lottery gets there on average, stride exactly). It is not optimised for turnaround or response time.
  • It tries to guarantee the lowest possible average turnaround time. Proportional share is explicitly not optimised for turnaround (or response). It targets percentages.
  • It tries to guarantee each job the same percentage, whatever its tickets. The share is proportional to tickets: 75 of 100 tickets → 75%.
  • It tries to guarantee each job a bounded response time. It is not optimised for response either. It guarantees a percentage of CPU time.

Lottery. The list is P (20 tickets) → Q (35) → R (45), the winning ticket is 40, and the walk stops when counter > winner. Which is TRUE?

  • Q runs: the counter goes 20, then 55, and 55 > 40. P: is 20 > 40? No. Q: is 55 > 40? Yes, stop. Q runs.
  • P runs: its counter of 20 is the first value below 40. Reversed test. The walk stops when the counter goes past the winner; 20 > 40 is false, so it keeps going.
  • R runs: it holds the most tickets, so the walk checks it first. The walk follows the list order (P, Q, R), not ticket size. Counter 20, then 55 > 40 → Q.
  • R runs: the counter goes 20, 55, then 100, which ends the walk. The walk stops at the first job whose counter passes the winner: 55 > 40, so Q.

Two jobs with equal tickets each need 40 time units. Under lottery, one finishes at t = 48 and the other at t = 80. Which is TRUE?

  • U = 48 / 80 = 0.6. U = (time the first job completes) / (time the second job completes) = 48/80 = 0.6. Perfectly fair would be 1.
  • U = 80 / 48 ≈ 1.67. Upside down. The first completion goes on top, so U ≤ 1: 48/80 = 0.6.
  • U = 40 / 80 = 0.5. 40 is the run-time, not a completion time. U = 48/80 = 0.6.
  • U = 40 / 48 ≈ 0.83. Both numbers must be completion times: U = 48/80 = 0.6.

Which is TRUE about how fair lottery scheduling is?

  • U gets close to 1 only when the jobs run for a long time. OSTEP's study: with short jobs U is poor; over a long run the random draws average out.
  • U gets close to 1 only when the jobs are short. Reversed. Short jobs mean few draws, so luck dominates. Long jobs → U near 1.
  • Lottery hits the exact ticket ratio in every short window of time. That is stride. Lottery is right only on average (Dr. Bilal's slide: B wins 4 of 15 draws with 25% of the tickets).
  • U close to 0 means the two jobs finished at nearly the same time. Finishing together gives U close to 1. U close to 0 is very unfair.

Which condition on line 36 matches the slides' "stop when counter > winner" with tickets numbered from 0?

  • winning_ticket < ticket_count counter > winner, written the other way round. P1 (count 60) owns 0–59.
  • winning_ticket <= ticket_count Off by one: ticket 60 would go to P1, but with numbering from 0, P1 owns only 0–59.
  • winning_ticket > ticket_count Reversed: P1 would win only when the draw is above its range.
  • winning_ticket < jobs[i].tickets That compares with this job's own tickets, not the running count. Draws 60–99 fail for P2 (< 30?) and P3 (< 10?), so they would match nobody.

P1 has finished. P2 (30 tickets) and P3 (10) are left, so total_tickets is 40. The draw is 30. Which is TRUE?

  • P3 runs: P2's count is 30 and 30 < 30 is false, so the walk reaches P3 (count 40). With numbering from 0, P2 owns 0–29 and P3 owns 30–39.
  • P2 runs: 30 is P2's last ticket, so it is in P2's range. That is numbering from 1 (P2 = 1–30). lottery.c numbers from 0, so P2 owns 0–29.
  • P1 runs: 30 is inside P1's old range 0–59. Line 34 skips finished jobs, and the ranges are renumbered without P1.
  • Nobody runs: 30 is outside every live job's range. P3's range is 30–39, so the draw does have an owner.

Which is TRUE about the ticket mechanisms?

  • Ticket transfer lets a client lend its tickets to a server that is working for it. The server runs faster on the client's behalf, then the tickets go back.
  • Ticket inflation lets a client lend its tickets to a server that is working for it. Lending tickets to another process is transfer. Inflation is a process raising or lowering its own ticket count.
  • Ticket currency lets a process raise its own ticket count when it needs more CPU. That is inflation. Currency lets a user split their tickets among their own jobs in local units, converted to global tickets.
  • Ticket inflation is safe even among processes that don't trust each other. Inflation only makes sense among processes that trust each other; a greedy process could give itself a huge number of tickets.

A user owns 60 global tickets and issues 400 tickets of their own currency: 100 to job J1 and 300 to job J2. Which is TRUE?

  • J1 holds 15 global tickets. global = local / user's total local × user's global = 100/400 × 60 = 15. (J2: 300/400 × 60 = 45.)
  • J1 holds 100 global tickets. 100 is J1's local count. Convert: 100/400 × 60 = 15.
  • J1 holds 25 global tickets. 25 is J1's percentage of the user's share (100/400 = 25%). Times 60 → 15.
  • J1 holds 45 global tickets. 45 is J2's value (300/400 × 60). J1 = 100/400 × 60 = 15.

Stride scheduling with a large number of 10,000. A has 40 tickets, B has 160. Which is TRUE?

  • A's stride is 250 and B's is 62.5, so B's pass grows more slowly and B runs more often. stride = 10,000 / tickets. B's smaller stride means its pass climbs slowly, so it is the lowest more often: 4 runs for every 1 of A's (160 : 40).
  • A's stride is 250 and B's is 62.5, so A's pass grows more slowly and A runs more often. A's bigger stride makes its pass grow faster, so A runs less often.
  • A's stride is 40 and B's is 160, so B's pass grows faster and A runs more often. Tickets aren't the stride. Stride = 10,000 / tickets: A 250, B 62.5.
  • A's stride is 62.5 and B's is 250, so A's pass grows more slowly and A runs more often. Inverted. Stride = BIG / tickets, so more tickets give a smaller stride: A = 10,000/40 = 250.

Which is TRUE about stride scheduling?

  • After a job runs, its pass increases by its stride. pass += stride, so jobs with more tickets (smaller stride) climb more slowly and run more often.
  • After a job runs, its pass increases by its tickets. It increases by its stride (BIG / tickets), not its ticket count.
  • After a job runs, its stride increases by its pass. Swapped: pass grows by the stride; the stride never changes.
  • After a job runs, the job with the highest pass runs next. The lowest pass runs next.

Stride, large number 1,000. A has 10 tickets (pass 300), B has 5 (pass 250), C has 20 (pass 380). Which is TRUE about the next pick?

  • B runs (lowest pass) and its pass becomes 450. B's stride = 1,000/5 = 200, so 250 + 200 = 450. A and C don't change.
  • C runs (smallest stride) and its pass becomes 430. The pick is by lowest pass, not smallest stride. B (250) runs.
  • B runs (lowest pass) and its pass becomes 255. Add the stride (1,000/5 = 200), not the tickets: 250 + 200 = 450.
  • B runs (lowest pass), and then every job's pass grows by its own stride. Only the job that ran updates its pass: B → 450, while A stays 300 and C stays 380.

Stride, large number 600. A has 4 tickets, B 2, C 6, listed A, B, C; ties go to the job listed first. Which is TRUE about the first six picks?

  • They are A B C C A C. Strides: A 150, B 300, C 100. Passes (A, B, C) before each pick: (0,0,0) A → (150,0,0) B → (150,300,0) C → (150,300,100) C → (150,300,200) A → (300,300,200) C.
  • They are C A B C A C. That breaks ties by most tickets. Ties go to the first listed: at (0,0,0) A runs, and at (150,0,0) B beats C.
  • They are C A C A B C. That starts each pass at its stride. Every job starts at pass 0, so the first pick is a three-way tie → A.
  • They are A B C B A B. That adds tickets (A +4, B +2, C +6) instead of strides, which favours the job with fewer tickets. Pass grows by the stride.

Which version of line 51's test makes ties go to the job listed first?

  • jobs[i].pass < jobs[min_pass_index].pass An equal pass doesn't replace the current minimum, so the earlier job keeps the win.
  • jobs[i].pass <= jobs[min_pass_index].pass An equal pass does replace it, so the last tied job wins.
  • jobs[i].pass > jobs[min_pass_index].pass That finds the highest pass. Stride runs the lowest.
  • jobs[i].stride < jobs[min_pass_index].stride That always picks the job with the most tickets. The pick is by pass, not stride.

In stride.c (strides A 100, B 200, C 1000), the passes before a pick are A 300, B 400, C 1000. Which is TRUE about the next two picks?

  • A, then A: A moves to 400, and the 400–400 tie goes to A, listed first. 300 is lowest → A runs → 300 + 100 = 400. Then A and B tie, and the strict < keeps A.
  • A, then B: A moves to 400, and the 400–400 tie goes to B, which waited longer. stride.c has no "waited longer" rule. A tie goes to the first listed: A.
  • A, then B: A moves to 500, so B's 400 is now the lowest. A adds its own stride (100), not B's (200): 300 + 100 = 400, a tie that A wins.
  • C, then A: C has run the fewest times, so it goes first. The pick is by lowest pass, not by run count. C's 1000 is the highest.

Which is TRUE about adding a new job part-way through?

  • Lottery just adds its tickets; in stride, a newcomer at pass 0 would monopolize the CPU. Everyone else's pass is already large, so a pass-0 newcomer is the lowest for a long time and wins every pick until it catches up.
  • Stride just starts it at pass 0; in lottery, a newcomer would monopolize the CPU. Swapped. Lottery keeps no per-job history, so a newcomer just adds tickets. It is stride where pass 0 hogs the CPU.
  • Lottery just adds its tickets; in stride, a newcomer at pass 0 would starve until it caught up. Reversed. The lowest pass runs, so a pass-0 newcomer runs every time (monopolizes) until it catches up.
  • Lottery just adds its tickets; in stride, every other job's stride must be recomputed. A stride is BIG / that job's own tickets; it doesn't depend on the total, so nobody else's stride changes. The problem is the newcomer's pass.

Which is TRUE when comparing lottery and stride scheduling?

  • Stride is deterministic and exact every cycle; lottery is right only on average over time. Stride keeps a pass per job and always picks the lowest, so proportions come out exactly. Lottery draws random winners.
  • Lottery is deterministic and exact every cycle; stride is right only on average over time. Swapped. Lottery draws random tickets; stride is the deterministic one.
  • Both are deterministic: once tickets are set, the same schedule repeats every run. Lottery is probabilistic: each slice's winner is a random draw.
  • Stride is deterministic and, like lottery, keeps no per-job global state. Stride keeps a pass for every job (global state). Lottery keeps only the tickets and the total.

Lesson 8 · Linux CFS: fair by the clock open lesson ↗

Dr. Bilal's recap explains why we move past lottery scheduling. Which is TRUE?

  • Lottery is probabilistic, so it is fair over a long run; over a short time, unlucky jobs suffer jitter (unfairness). Random draws even out only over many draws. In the short term some jobs lose more than their share: that is the jitter.
  • Lottery is probabilistic, so it is fair over a short run; over a long time, unlucky jobs suffer jitter (unfairness). Reversed. Luck evens out over many draws, so lottery is fair in the long run and unfair in the short term.
  • Stride is probabilistic, so it is fair over a long run; over a short time, unlucky jobs suffer jitter (unfairness). Wrong scheduler. Stride is deterministic (lowest pass runs), so it has no jitter; lottery is the probabilistic one.
  • Lottery is deterministic, so it is fair over a long run; over a short time, unlucky jobs suffer jitter (unfairness). A deterministic scheduler has no "unlucky" jobs. Lottery picks a random winning ticket: it is probabilistic.

CFS tries to imitate an "ideal fair CPU". Which is TRUE?

  • With N runnable tasks, all N run at once, each at exactly 1/N of the CPU's speed; CFS fakes this with quick time slices. That is the ideal (perfectly divisible) CPU. A real core runs one task at a time, so CFS switches quickly so each task's real time matches its ideal share.
  • With N runnable tasks, all N run at once, each at the CPU's full speed; CFS fakes this with quick time slices. The N tasks share one CPU, so each gets 1/N of its speed, not full speed.
  • With N runnable tasks, all N run at once, each at exactly 1/N of the CPU's speed; CFS fakes this with random ticket draws. Random draws are lottery, which CFS replaces. CFS is deterministic and uses time slices and vruntime, not tickets.
  • With N runnable tasks, all N run at once, each at exactly 1/N of the CPU's speed; CFS fakes this by running each task to completion. Running each task to the end is FIFO-like and unfair in the short term. CFS switches quickly between tasks with small time slices.

Which is TRUE about CFS's vruntime?

  • The task with the smallest vruntime runs next; vruntime grows as the task runs. Whoever has had the least (weighted) CPU time so far is next in line. Waiting in the run queue adds nothing.
  • The task with the largest vruntime runs next; vruntime grows as the task runs. The smallest vruntime runs: the task furthest behind goes next.
  • The task with the smallest vruntime runs next; vruntime also grows while it waits in the run queue. Waiting for the CPU adds no vruntime; only running does. That is how a waiting task falls behind and gets picked.
  • The task with the largest weight runs next; vruntime grows as the task runs. The pick is always the smallest vruntime. Weight only changes how fast vruntime grows.

Which is TRUE about Linux nice values?

  • They range from −20 to +19, and −20 is the highest priority. Lower nice = "less nice to others" = bigger weight = more CPU.
  • They range from −20 to +19, and +19 is the highest priority. +19 is the lowest priority (a "nice" process gives way). −20 is the highest.
  • They range from −20 to +19, and a higher nice value means a bigger weight. Reversed: lower nice → bigger weight (−5 → 3121, 0 → 1024, +5 → 335).
  • They range from −20 to +19, and a nice −20 task's vruntime grows fastest. Biggest weight → smallest 1024/weight → vruntime grows slowest.

Which is TRUE about CFS weights?

  • Nice 0 has weight 1024, and each nice step changes the weight by about 1.25×. 1024 is weight0 in the vruntime formula; nice +1 → 820 and nice −1 → 1277, about 1.25× apart.
  • Nice 0 has weight 1024, and each nice step changes the weight by about 2×. About 1.25× per step: 1024 → 820 (nice +1), 1024 → 1277 (nice −1).
  • Nice 0 has weight 0, so its vruntime grows at the same rate as real time. Its weight is 1024 (= weight0); that's why its vruntime matches real time: runtime × 1024/1024.
  • Nice 0 has weight 1024, and a nice +5 task has a bigger weight than that. Higher nice → smaller weight: nice +5 → 335.

X (nice −5, weight 3121) and Y (nice 0, weight 1024) are the only tasks. X runs for 15 ms. Which is TRUE about X's vruntime?

  • It grows by about 4.92 ms. vruntime += runtime × weight0/weightX = 15 × 1024/3121 = 15360/3121 ≈ 4.92 ms.
  • It grows by about 45.72 ms. Fraction upside down: 15 × 3121/1024. It is weight0/weightX: 15 × 1024/3121 ≈ 4.92.
  • It grows by exactly 15 ms. Only a nice 0 task gains its real runtime. X's weight is 3121: 15 × 1024/3121 ≈ 4.92.
  • It grows by about 3.71 ms. That divides by the sum of weights (15 × 1024/4145), which belongs in the time-slice formula. vruntime uses 1024/3121: ≈ 4.92.

Which is TRUE about a high-priority (big-weight) task in CFS?

  • Its vruntime grows more slowly than real time, so it stays left in the tree and is picked more often. Big weight → 1024/weight < 1 → slow clock → small vruntime → leftmost → runs again soon.
  • Its vruntime grows faster than real time, so it is picked more often. Big weight → 1024/weight < 1 → slower. A fast-growing vruntime would make it picked less.
  • Its vruntime grows more slowly than real time, so it drifts right in the tree. Small vruntimes stay on the left, which is where CFS picks from.
  • Its vruntime grows at real-time speed, but CFS picks big weights first. The pick rule never changes (smallest vruntime). Weight only changes the speed of the task's clock.

CFS with sched_latency = 24 ms and min_granularity = 4 ms. A (nice 0, weight 1024), B (nice −5, weight 3121), C (nice +5, weight 335). Which is TRUE about B's time slice?

  • It is about 16.72 ms. Σ weights = 1024 + 3121 + 335 = 4480. B = 3121/4480 × 24 ≈ 16.72 ms, well above the 4 ms floor.
  • It is exactly 8 ms. An equal split (24/3) ignores the weights. Slice ∝ weight: 3121/4480 × 24 ≈ 16.72.
  • It is about 73.15 ms. That divides by weight0 (3121/1024 × 24). Divide by the sum of weights, 4480: ≈ 16.72.
  • It is about 7.87 ms. That is 24 × 1024/3121, the vruntime fraction. Slice = weight/Σ weights × latency ≈ 16.72.

Same tasks (sched_latency = 24 ms, min_granularity = 4 ms), all starting at vruntime 0. Each runs one slice. Which is TRUE?

  • C ends highest at about 12.23, because its 1.79 ms slice was raised to 4 ms; A and B both end at about 5.49. C: 335/4480 × 24 ≈ 1.79 < 4, so it runs 4 ms → 4 × 1024/335 ≈ 12.23. A: 5.49 × 1024/1024 = 5.49. B: 16.72 × 1024/3121 ≈ 5.49.
  • All three end at about 5.49, because each round gives every task the same vruntime. That holds only for unclamped slices. C ran 4 ms, not 1.79, so it gains 4 × 1024/335 ≈ 12.23.
  • B ends highest at about 16.72, because it ran the longest; A and C end lower. 16.72 is B's real runtime; its vruntime is 16.72 × 1024/3121 ≈ 5.49. C (clamped up) ends highest at ≈ 12.23.
  • C ends lowest at about 1.79, because it ran the shortest slice. Two slips: C's slice is raised to 4 ms, and its vruntime is scaled by 1024/335: 4 × 1024/335 ≈ 12.23, the highest.

20 runnable tasks, all nice 0. sched_latency = 48 ms, min_granularity = 6 ms. Which is TRUE?

  • Each slice is 6 ms and one full round takes 120 ms. 48/20 = 2.4 ms is below the 6 ms floor, so each task gets 6 ms; 20 × 6 = 120 ms.
  • Each slice is 2.4 ms and one full round takes 48 ms. Forgot the floor: 2.4 < 6, so each slice is raised to 6 ms and the round becomes 120 ms.
  • Each slice is 6 ms and one full round still takes 48 ms. Twenty 6 ms slices can't fit in 48 ms; the round stretches to 20 × 6 = 120 ms.
  • Each slice is 6 ms, so only 8 of the 20 tasks run in each round. Every runnable task still runs once per round; the round just stretches to 120 ms.

Which is TRUE about CFS's red-black tree?

  • It is keyed by vruntime, and the leftmost node is the next task to run. Smaller keys sit on the left, so the leftmost node holds the smallest vruntime.
  • It is keyed by vruntime, and the rightmost node is the next task to run. The rightmost node has the largest vruntime. CFS runs the leftmost.
  • It is keyed by weight, and the leftmost node is the next task to run. The key is vruntime. Weight only sets how fast a task's vruntime grows.
  • It is keyed by vruntime, and the root node is the next task to run. The root is just a middle value. The smallest is the leftmost node.

Which is TRUE about inserting a waking task into CFS's red-black tree of n runnable tasks?

  • It costs O(log n), because a balanced tree has height about log₂ n. Insertion walks one root-to-leaf path and rebalances; OSTEP: insertion and deletion are logarithmic.
  • It costs O(n), because the tree must be walked in order to find the spot. That is the cost for a sorted list. A balanced search tree follows one path: O(log n).
  • It costs O(1), because the kernel caches a pointer to the leftmost node. The cached pointer makes picking fast. Inserting still descends the tree: O(log n).
  • It costs O(n log n), because the whole tree is re-sorted after each insert. Nothing is re-sorted: one insert plus a local rebalance, O(log n).

The CFS tree holds tasks with vruntimes 14.2, 9.6 and 22.0 ms. A brand-new task is created. Which is TRUE?

  • It starts at 9.6, the current min_vruntime. New and waking tasks get the smallest vruntime in the tree, so they compete fairly from now on.
  • It starts at 0, the lowest possible vruntime. At 0 it would be far behind everyone and monopolize the CPU while catching up. CFS uses min_vruntime: 9.6.
  • It starts at about 15.27, the average vruntime in the tree. CFS uses the minimum, not the average: 9.6.
  • It starts at 22.0, the largest vruntime, so it waits its turn. That would put it behind everyone. CFS uses the minimum: 9.6.

Which is TRUE about how each scheduler chooses the next job?

  • Lottery draws a random winning ticket, stride runs the job with the lowest pass, and CFS runs the task with the lowest vruntime. Matches the table: random ticket / lowest pass / lowest vruntime (the leftmost node of the red-black tree).
  • Lottery draws a random winning ticket, stride runs the job with the lowest stride, and CFS runs the task with the lowest vruntime. The stride is a fixed step (BIG / tickets). Stride picks the lowest pass, the running total of strides.
  • Lottery draws a random winning ticket, stride runs the job with the highest pass, and CFS runs the task with the lowest vruntime. Reversed. The job that has run least (relative to its tickets) has the lowest pass, and that one runs.
  • Lottery runs the job holding the most tickets, stride runs the job with the lowest pass, and CFS runs the task with the lowest vruntime. That would let the biggest ticket-holder run every time. Lottery draws a random ticket; more tickets only raise the chance of winning.

Which is TRUE about what each scheduler updates after a job runs?

  • Lottery updates nothing; stride adds BIG / tickets to the job's pass; CFS adds runtime × 1024 / weight to its vruntime. Matches the table. Lottery just draws again; stride's step shrinks with more tickets; CFS's vruntime grows more slowly for bigger weights.
  • Lottery updates nothing; stride adds BIG × tickets to the job's pass; CFS adds runtime × 1024 / weight to its vruntime. The stride is BIG ÷ tickets. More tickets must mean a smaller step, so the job is picked more often.
  • Lottery updates nothing; stride adds BIG / tickets to the job's pass; CFS adds runtime × weight / 1024 to its vruntime. Inverted. It is runtime × 1024 / weight, so a big-weight (high-priority) task's vruntime grows more slowly.
  • Lottery removes the winning ticket; stride adds BIG / tickets to the job's pass; CFS adds runtime × 1024 / weight to its vruntime. Lottery keeps every ticket in play; the next draw is from the same tickets. It has nothing to update.

If stride.c were turned into CFS, which line would become vruntime += runtime × 1024 / weight?

  • Line 65, pass += stride. It is the update after the job runs: the counter grows by a weighted amount.
  • Line 28, stride = NUMERATOR / tickets. That runs once, at the start, to set the step size. The per-slice update is line 65.
  • Line 51, the pass < comparison. That is the pick rule (lowest counter wins), not the update.
  • Line 64, remaining_time--. That tracks how much work is left. CFS's vruntime update corresponds to the pass update, line 65.

stride.c starts every job at pass 0 (line 29). Which is TRUE about doing that for a task that joins later?

  • In stride it would monopolize the CPU until it caught up; CFS avoids this by starting it at min_vruntime. Everyone else's counter is already large, so 0 is the lowest by far. CFS starts newcomers at the smallest vruntime in the tree.
  • In stride it would starve until it caught up; CFS avoids this by starting it at min_vruntime. The lowest counter runs, so a pass-0 newcomer runs every time. It hogs the CPU; it doesn't starve.
  • In stride it would monopolize the CPU until it caught up; CFS also starts it at 0. CFS sets a new task's vruntime to min_vruntime, not 0, for exactly this reason.
  • In stride it would monopolize the CPU until it caught up; CFS starts it at the largest vruntime. That would make it wait behind everyone. CFS uses the minimum.

Lesson 9 · Scheduling on many CPUs open lesson ↗

Which is TRUE about temporal locality?

  • Data used once is likely to be used again soon, like a loop counter. Temporal = the same data again, soon. Caches keep it, so the second use is a hit.
  • Data near something just used is likely to be used next, like an array walk. That is spatial locality. Temporal is about the same data used again soon.
  • Data used once is unlikely to be needed again soon, so caches evict it. Reversed. Caches work because recently used data is likely to be used again.
  • A process that ran on a CPU is likely to run on that same CPU again soon. That describes cache affinity, a scheduling goal. Temporal locality is about a program reusing data.

A loop adds a[0], a[1], a[2], … into a variable sum. Which is TRUE?

  • Reading a[i+1] just after a[i] is spatial locality; reusing sum every pass is temporal. Neighbouring addresses = spatial; the same variable again soon = temporal.
  • Reading a[i+1] just after a[i] is temporal locality; reusing sum every pass is spatial. Swapped. Neighbours = spatial; same data again = temporal.
  • Both are spatial locality, because all the data sits next to each other in memory. sum is not a neighbour being read; it is the same variable reused: temporal.
  • Both are temporal locality, because the loop repeats the same steps. Each array element is read only once; what helps is that it is next to the previous one: spatial.

Which is TRUE about cache coherence on a multiprocessor?

  • Bus snooping, done in hardware, makes caches invalidate or update their copy when another CPU writes it. Each cache watches the shared bus; on seeing a write to an address it holds, it invalidates or updates its copy.
  • Bus snooping, done by the OS scheduler, makes caches invalidate or update their copy when another CPU writes it. Snooping is done by the hardware, invisible to the OS and to your code.
  • Bus snooping, done in hardware, also makes multi-step updates like List_Pop() safe without locks. Coherence keeps single values consistent. A multi-step update still needs a lock, or two CPUs can pop and free the same node.
  • Coherence is not an issue, because all the CPUs share one cache. Each CPU has its own private cache over a shared memory; that is exactly why stale copies appear.

Which is TRUE about cache affinity?

  • A process runs faster if it runs again on the same CPU, whose cache still holds its state. Its data is still warm in that CPU's cache (and TLB), so keep a process on the same CPU whenever possible.
  • A process runs faster if it moves to a different CPU, whose cache has free room. A different CPU's cache is cold for it, so it must reload everything. Stay on the same CPU.
  • A process should go to whichever CPU has the fewest jobs; that is what affinity means. That is load balancing. Affinity = keep a process on the same CPU when possible.
  • A process runs faster on the same CPU because only that CPU can reach its memory. All CPUs share main memory. The gain comes from the warm cache (and TLB).

Why does single-queue multiprocessor scheduling (SQMS) scale poorly? Which is TRUE?

  • Every CPU must take the same queue lock, so lock contention grows as CPUs are added. More CPUs means more of them waiting for the one lock, until the scheduler itself is the bottleneck.
  • Each CPU's queue can become unbalanced, so some CPUs sit idle. That is MQMS's problem. SQMS has one queue, so load balances naturally; its problem is the shared lock.
  • Jobs never move between CPUs, so busy CPUs can't share their work. Opposite: in SQMS jobs move constantly (poor affinity). Scalability suffers from lock contention.
  • Every CPU must take the same queue lock, so cache coherence breaks as CPUs are added. Coherence is kept by hardware snooping. The cost is CPUs waiting for the lock.

SQMS with five jobs A–E on four CPUs: every time slice, each CPU takes the next job from the shared queue. Which is TRUE about job A?

  • A lands on a different CPU every time, so it keeps starting with a cold cache. A goes CPU 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → … and never reuses a warm cache. That is SQMS's poor cache affinity.
  • A stays on CPU 0, because SQMS keeps each job on the CPU it started on. Plain SQMS has no such rule; A bounces CPU 0 → 1 → 2 → 3. Keeping jobs in place needs an extra affinity mechanism.
  • A lands on a different CPU every time, which keeps its cache warm on all four. Other jobs fill each cache in between, so A starts cold each time.
  • A lands on a different CPU every time, but that costs only lock time, not cache warmth. Moving costs cache warmth (affinity). Lock contention is SQMS's other, separate problem.

Which is TRUE about multi-queue multiprocessor scheduling (MQMS)?

  • It fixes SQMS's lock contention and poor cache affinity, but it can suffer load imbalance. One queue per CPU: no global lock, and jobs stay put. But one queue can end up with more jobs than another.
  • It fixes SQMS's load imbalance and poor cache affinity, but it suffers lock contention. Swapped. SQMS balances load naturally; MQMS has no global lock but can become imbalanced.
  • It fixes SQMS's lock contention, but it makes cache affinity worse. Jobs stay on their own queue, so they keep running on the same CPU: better affinity.
  • It fixes lock contention, cache affinity and load imbalance with no extra mechanism. Load imbalance is MQMS's new problem; it needs migration (e.g. work stealing).

MQMS, two CPUs, round robin, no load balancing. Q0 holds only A; Q1 holds B, C, D and E. Over a long run, which is TRUE?

  • A gets 4 times as much CPU as B. A has CPU 0 to itself (1 CPU). B shares CPU 1 with C, D and E (1/4 CPU). 1 ÷ 1/4 = 4.
  • A gets 3 times as much CPU as B. B shares CPU 1 with three others, so 4 jobs split it: B gets 1/4 and 1 ÷ 1/4 = 4.
  • Every job gets 2/5 of a CPU, because two CPUs are shared by five jobs. That would need load balancing. Without it, each CPU only round-robins its own queue: A gets 1, the others 1/4.

MQMS: CPU 0 runs only A; CPU 1 runs B and D. Which is TRUE?

  • Migrating one job once just flips the imbalance; continuous migration keeps switching which job moves. Over time A, B and D then each get about the same share of the two CPUs.
  • Migrating B to CPU 0 once fixes it, since both CPUs then have work. Then CPU 0 has A and B while D is alone on CPU 1: the same imbalance, flipped. Keep switching which job moves.
  • Nothing can help, because three jobs can't share two CPUs fairly. Over time they can: continuous migration gives A, B and D about the same share.
  • A should be pinned to CPU 0 for good, to protect its cache affinity. Then A keeps getting twice the CPU of B and D. The fix is continuous migration.

Which is TRUE about work stealing?

  • A queue that is low on jobs peeks at a fuller queue now and then, and steals jobs from it. The source (low) queue occasionally peeks at a target queue; if the target is notably fuller, it takes one or more jobs.
  • A queue that is full peeks at an emptier queue now and then, and pushes jobs onto it. In work stealing the source is the queue that is low on jobs, and it takes work from the fuller target.
  • A queue that is low on jobs peeks at the others constantly, which costs almost nothing. Peeking too often brings back the overhead and scaling trouble MQMS was built to avoid. Too rarely, and load stays unbalanced.
  • A queue that is low on jobs steals from a fuller queue, and the stolen job keeps its warm cache. The stolen job moves to a new CPU and starts cold. Stealing trades a little affinity for balance.

Which is TRUE about Linux's multiprocessor schedulers?

  • O(1) and CFS use multiple queues; BFS uses a single queue. OSTEP: both O(1) and CFS use multiple queues, whereas BFS uses a single queue, showing both approaches can work.
  • O(1) and BFS use multiple queues; CFS uses a single queue. CFS is multi-queue. BFS is the single-queue one.
  • CFS and BFS use multiple queues; O(1) uses a single queue. O(1) is multi-queue. BFS is the single-queue one.
  • All three use one queue per CPU, as in MQMS. BFS is the exception: a single queue.

Lesson 10 · The address space open lesson ↗

Which statement about memory in early systems (before multiprogramming) is TRUE?

  • The OS was a library of routines in memory, one running program used the rest, and the program saw physical memory directly. OSTEP 13.1: early machines gave users little abstraction. With only one program and no sharing, there was nothing to protect it from.
  • The OS was a library of routines in memory, several programs shared the rest, and each program saw physical memory directly. Wrong era. Several programs in memory at once is multiprogramming, which came later. Early systems ran one program.
  • The OS was a library of routines in memory, one running program used the rest, and the program saw a virtual address space starting at 0. The virtual address space is the later abstraction. Early machines had no such illusion: the program used physical memory directly.
  • The OS was a library of routines in memory, one running program used the rest, and its memory was saved to disk on every switch. Saving all of memory to disk on each switch was the crude time-sharing idea, which came later (and was too slow). Early systems ran one program with no switching.

Which statement about multiprogramming is TRUE?

  • Several processes are ready at once, and the OS switches when one does I/O, to raise CPU utilization; it came before time sharing. OSTEP 13.2: machines were expensive, so keeping the CPU busy during I/O mattered. Time sharing (interactivity) came after.
  • Several processes are ready at once, and the OS switches when one does I/O, to give users an interactive response; it came before time sharing. Wrong goal. Quick interactive response is the goal of time sharing; multiprogramming's goal is better CPU utilization.
  • Several processes are ready at once, and the OS switches only when one finishes, to raise CPU utilization; it came before time sharing. Wrong trigger. The OS switches when a process waits (e.g. for I/O), so the CPU isn't left idle.
  • Several processes are ready at once, and the OS switches when one does I/O, to raise CPU utilization; it came after time sharing. Wrong order. Multiprogramming came first; people then demanded more, and time sharing followed.

Which statement about the address space is TRUE?

  • It is the running program's view of memory: a private range of addresses starting at 0, holding its code, heap and stack. This is the abstraction the OS provides (OSTEP §13.2): every process gets its own, and every address in it is virtual.
  • It is the running program's view of memory: a private range of addresses starting where the OS loaded it in physical RAM. It starts at 0. Where the process really sits (e.g. 320KB) is hidden from it; that's what translation is for.
  • It is the slice of physical RAM the OS reserves for a process, holding its code, heap and stack at their real addresses. That's the physical memory behind it. The address space is the program's view of memory, made of virtual addresses.
  • It is the running program's view of memory: one range of addresses starting at 0 that all running processes share. Each process gets its own private address space; sharing one would destroy protection.

In the 16KB example address space (OSTEP / Dr. Bilal), which statement about the code segment is TRUE?

  • It is static (its size is fixed while the program runs), so it is placed at the start of the address space, at address 0. OSTEP §13.3: the code is static and easy to place, so it goes at the top (address 0); it never needs room to grow.
  • It grows on every function call, so it is placed at the start of the address space, at address 0. That's the stack. The code is static: the instructions don't change size while running.
  • It is static (its size is fixed while the program runs), so it is placed at the far end of the address space, at 16KB. The stack sits at the far end. Code sits at the start, address 0.
  • It is static (its size is fixed while the program runs), so it is placed in the free gap between the heap and the stack. The free gap is left empty so the heap and stack can grow into it. Code sits at address 0.

Which statement about how the heap and the stack grow is TRUE?

  • The heap grows toward higher addresses and the stack toward lower addresses, so the two grow toward each other. Heap starts just after the code and grows positively; stack starts at the far end and grows negatively. They share the free gap.
  • The heap grows toward lower addresses and the stack toward higher addresses, so the two grow toward each other. Swapped. Heap grows toward higher addresses, stack toward lower. (Zafar's "stack grows down" drawing means the same thing.)
  • The heap grows toward higher addresses and the stack toward lower addresses, so the two grow away from each other. They start at opposite ends, so growing that way brings them toward each other, into the shared gap.
  • The heap and the stack both grow toward higher addresses, and the stack starts just after the end of the heap. The stack starts at the far end and grows toward lower addresses.

Process C sits in physical memory at 128KB–192KB, but believes its address space starts at 0. C executes load from address 1000. Which is TRUE?

  • 1000 is a virtual address; the load really reads physical 131,072 + 1,000 = 132,072. 128KB = 128 × 1024 = 131,072. The OS and hardware add C's real starting point to every address it uses.
  • 1000 is a physical address; the load really reads physical 1,000, which belongs to the OS. Every address a program uses is virtual. Reading the OS's memory is exactly what translation prevents.
  • 1000 is a virtual address; the load really reads physical 128,000 + 1,000 = 129,000. KB means 1024 here: 128KB = 131,072, so the answer is 132,072.
  • 1000 is a virtual address; the load really reads physical 196,608 + 1,000 = 197,608. 196,608 is 192KB, C's end. Virtual 0 maps to C's start, 128KB, so the answer is 132,072.

Which statement about ASLR is TRUE?

  • Address Space Layout Randomization: code, heap and stack get different random virtual addresses each run, so attackers can't predict them. That's why va_explorer prints different code, heap and stack addresses on every run. It is a security feature.
  • Address Space Layout Randomization: code, heap and stack get different random virtual addresses each run, so processes never clash in RAM. Keeping processes apart in RAM is the job of address translation. ASLR exists for security: unpredictable addresses.
  • Address Space Layout Randomization: only the heap gets a different random virtual address each run; code and stack stay fixed. All three move: in the lesson's two runs the code (0x63a4… vs 0x5d0e…) and the stack changed too.
  • Address Space Layout Randomization: the process is put at a different random physical address each run, and the program prints it. Printed pointers are always virtual. ASLR randomises the virtual layout of the address space.

With ASLR off, two copies of the same program both print the heap address 0x5555555592a0, yet each one counts up independently. Which conclusion is TRUE?

  • The printed address is virtual: the same virtual address maps to different physical memory in each process. Two processes can't own the same physical RAM, so each one's 0x…92a0 is translated to its own physical location.
  • The printed address is virtual: the same virtual address maps to the same physical memory in both processes. Then one process's writes would show up in the other's counter. They count independently, so the physical memory is different.
  • The printed address is physical: the OS gives both processes the same physical block and saves it on every switch. Pointers you print are virtual. Swapping memory to disk on every switch is the slow approach the OS avoids.
  • The printed address is physical, and the two values only match because ASLR is turned off. ASLR changes the virtual layout. Printed pointers are never physical; matching values prove they're virtual.

Inside main(): double *d = malloc(sizeof(double)); *d = 2.5;
Which statement is TRUE?

  • d holds a heap address, &d is a stack address, and *d is 2.5, stored in the heap. d holds what malloc returned (heap). d itself is a local, so its own address &d is on the stack. *d follows d to the heap value.
  • d holds a stack address, &d is a heap address, and *d is 2.5, stored in the heap. Swapped: d holds what malloc returned, a heap address; &d is where d itself lives, on the stack.
  • d holds a heap address, &d is a stack address, and *d is 2.5, stored on the stack. *d is the value at the address d holds, so it is stored in the heap.
  • d holds a heap address, &d is that same heap address, and *d is 2.5, stored in the heap. &d is the address of the pointer variable d itself, a stack address, different from the heap address inside it.

At file scope: int *g; Then main() runs g = malloc(4 * sizeof(int)); g[0] = 7;
Which statement is TRUE?

  • &g is in the data (globals) region, g holds a heap address, and *g is 7. g is a global, so g itself lives in the data region (strictly .bss, the zero-filled part for uninitialised globals). Its value is what malloc returned (heap). *g is g[0] = 7.
  • &g is on the stack, g holds a heap address, and *g is 7. Only local variables live on the stack. g is a global, so &g is in the data region.
  • &g is in the data (globals) region, g holds a data-region address, and *g is 7. Where g lives doesn't change what it holds: it holds malloc's return value, a heap address.
  • &g is in the data (globals) region, g holds a heap address, and *g is the address of g[0]. The address of g[0] is g itself. *g is the value g[0], which is 7.

In mem.c, which line stores a value into the heap block?

  • Line 19, *p = atoi(argv[1]);: it follows p to the heap and writes the int there. The * means "the thing p points at", which is the heap int.
  • Line 13, p = malloc(sizeof(int));: it follows p to the heap and writes the int there. Line 13 writes into p itself (on the stack): it stores the heap address, not a value in the block.
  • Line 17, printf(..., (void *)p);: it follows p to the heap and writes the int there. Line 17 only reads p (the address) to print it. Nothing is written.
  • Line 12, int *p;: it follows p to the heap and writes the int there. Line 12 just declares the pointer on the stack. It doesn't point anywhere yet.

You run ./mem 20. Which is TRUE about the first "value of p" line?

  • It prints 21, about one second after the program starts. Each pass sleeps (line 21), adds 1 (line 22), then prints (line 23).
  • It prints 20, about one second after the program starts. Line 22 adds 1 before line 23 prints, so the first value is already 21.
  • It prints 21, immediately when the program starts. sleep(1) on line 21 runs first in every loop pass, so there's a one-second wait.
  • It prints 22, about one second after the program starts. Only one increment (line 22) happens before the first print: 20 + 1 = 21.

In va_explorer.c, line 22 prints (void *)&hhh where int hhh = 42; is a local. Which is TRUE?

  • It prints the virtual address of hhh, which is on the stack (0x7ff… on Linux). & gives the address of the variable. hhh is a local, so it's on the stack, and every printed pointer is virtual.
  • It prints the virtual address of hhh, which is in the heap (0x5… on Linux). Only malloc'd memory is on the heap. A local variable lives on the stack.
  • It prints the physical address of hhh, which is on the stack (0x7ff… on Linux). A program never sees physical addresses: every pointer it prints is virtual.
  • It prints the value of hhh, which is 42, stored on the stack. That would be hhh with %d. &hhh with %p is its address.

Which description of the three goals of virtual memory is TRUE?

  • Transparency: the program can't tell memory is virtualized. Efficiency: little time or space overhead. Protection: no process can touch another's memory or the OS's. These are the T·E·P goals (OSTEP §13.5, Bilal Ch 13 p.19). Bilal lists them in the order P, E, T; the meanings are the same.
  • Transparency: the program can see which physical addresses it uses. Efficiency: little time or space overhead. Protection: no process can touch another's memory or the OS's. Transparent means invisible: the program should not be able to tell memory is virtualized.
  • Transparency: the program can't tell memory is virtualized. Efficiency: little time overhead; space overhead doesn't matter. Protection: no process can touch another's memory or the OS's. Efficiency covers both time (speed) and space (little memory spent on bookkeeping).
  • Transparency: the program can't tell memory is virtualized. Efficiency: little time or space overhead. Protection: no process can touch another's memory, though it may read the OS's. Protection isolates processes from each other and from the OS.

A proposed VM design is safe and invisible to programs, but the OS checks and translates every memory access in software, so each access is 30× slower. Which is TRUE?

  • It fails the efficiency goal (time); translation has to be done by hardware so it costs almost nothing per access. Every fetch, load and store is translated, so it must be fast: that's why it needs hardware support.
  • It fails the efficiency goal (space); the OS's bookkeeping for the checks wastes too much memory. The problem described is speed: it fails efficiency in time.
  • It fails the protection goal; a check done in software lets a process reach another process's memory. The design is stated to be safe. What it loses is efficiency (time).
  • It fails the efficiency goal (time); the fix is to translate addresses only at context switches, not on every access. Every access must be translated. The fix is to do it in hardware.

Lesson 11 · malloc, free, and how they go wrong open lesson ↗

With 4-byte ints:
void f(void) {
    int n = 4;
    int *q = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    q[0] = 1;
}
Right after f returns, which is TRUE?
  • n and q are gone with the stack frame, but the 16-byte block q pointed to is still allocated on the heap. Locals live on the stack and die at return; heap memory lasts until free(). 4 × 4 = 16 bytes, now leaked.
  • n and q are gone with the stack frame, but the 4-byte block q pointed to is still allocated on the heap. The block holds n ints: 4 × sizeof(int) = 4 × 4 = 16 bytes, not 4.
  • n and q are gone with the stack frame, and the 16-byte block q pointed to is freed along with them. C has no garbage collector. A heap block is freed only by free(); here it is leaked.
  • n is gone with the stack frame, but q and the 16-byte block it points to are still allocated on the heap. q is a local variable, so q itself is on the stack and dies at return. Only *q (the block) is on the heap.

A function reads n from the user, then builds an array of n ints that its caller will keep using. Which is TRUE?

  • Use malloc(n * sizeof(int)): the heap block outlives the function, and the caller must free() it later. The data must outlive the function and its size is known only at run time: both are reasons to use the heap.
  • Use a local array int a[n]: the stack block outlives the function, and the caller must free() it later. A local array is on the stack and is freed when the function returns; returning it gives a dangling pointer (and you never free stack memory).
  • Use malloc(n * sizeof(int)): the heap block outlives the function, and it is freed when the caller returns. Heap memory is never freed automatically; the caller (or someone) must call free().
  • Use malloc(n): the heap block outlives the function, and the caller must free() it later. malloc takes bytes. n ints need n × sizeof(int) bytes (4n with 4-byte ints), not n.

What does malloc(n) return?

  • On success, a void * to a block of n bytes on the heap; on failure, NULL, so you should check the result. Bilal Ch 14 p.2: success → void pointer to the block; fail → a null pointer.
  • On success, a void * to a block of n bytes on the heap; on failure, nothing: the program is terminated. malloc returns NULL on failure and the program carries on, which is why you must check.
  • On success, a void * to a block of n bytes on the heap, all set to zero; on failure, NULL. malloc does not clear the block (that's the "forgot to initialize" bug). calloc zeroes.
  • On success, an int * to a block of n ints on the heap; on failure, NULL. The argument is a number of bytes, and the return type is void *. For n ints, ask for n * sizeof(int).

char *src = "kernel"; You want a heap copy made with strcpy. How many bytes must you malloc?

  • 7: strlen("kernel") is 6, and the '\0' terminator needs one more byte. C strings end with an invisible '\0' that strlen doesn't count, so malloc(strlen(src) + 1) = 7.
  • 6: strlen("kernel") is 6, and that count already includes the '\0' terminator. strlen does not count the '\0'. You need 6 + 1 = 7.
  • 6: strlen("kernel") is 6, and strcpy puts the '\0' just past the block, which is allowed. Writing that byte past the block is a buffer overflow (it may seem to work, then corrupt something). Allocate 7.
  • 8: sizeof(src) is 8 on a 64-bit machine, and that is the number of bytes the string takes. sizeof(src) is the size of the pointer, not of the string. Use strlen(src) + 1 = 7.

On a 64-bit machine with 4-byte ints: int *a = malloc(20 * sizeof(int)); int b[20];
Which is TRUE?

  • sizeof(a) is 8 and sizeof(b) is 80. a is a pointer, so you get the pointer's size (8). b is a real array, so you get 20 × 4 = 80.
  • sizeof(a) is 80 and sizeof(b) is 80. a is a pointer: sizeof gives the pointer's size, 8, never the size of the block it points to.
  • sizeof(a) is 8 and sizeof(b) is 8. b is a real array whose size is known at compile time: sizeof(b) = 20 × 4 = 80.
  • sizeof(a) is 4 and sizeof(b) is 80. 4 is a pointer on a 32-bit machine (as on the slides). On a 64-bit machine a pointer is 8 bytes.

You need a heap block for exactly n ints, no more and no less. Which line is TRUE (correct)?

  • int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int)); malloc counts bytes: n ints need n × 4 bytes on a machine with 4-byte ints.
  • int *arr = malloc(n); That's n bytes, a quarter of what n ints need: a buffer overflow waiting to happen.
  • int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(arr)); sizeof(arr) is the size of the pointer (8 on 64-bit), not of an int, so it asks for twice the bytes. Use sizeof(int) (or sizeof *arr).
  • int *arr = malloc(sizeof(int)); That's room for just one int. Multiply by n.

Line 29 passes &arr[i] to scanf. Which expression gives the same address?

  • arr + i Pointer arithmetic already scales by sizeof(int), so arr + i is the address of element i in the heap.
  • arr + i * sizeof(int) That scales twice: it lands at element 4i, far past where you meant.
  • &arr + i &arr is the address of the pointer variable on the stack, not of the heap block.
  • arr[i] That's the value of element i, not its address. scanf needs an address.

Right after free(p); which statement is TRUE?

  • The block is marked free so a later malloc can reuse it, and p still holds the same address. free() only updates the allocator's bookkeeping. It can't change p (p is passed by value), so p now dangles.
  • The block is marked free so a later malloc can reuse it, and p is set to NULL automatically. free() does not touch your pointer. Set p = NULL; yourself.
  • The block's bytes are erased and handed back to the OS, and p still holds the same address. free() does not erase the data and usually keeps the memory in the library's free list, not the OS.
  • The block is unmapped from the process, so any later use of *p is guaranteed to crash. The memory usually stays mapped, so using *p often seems to work. That's why use-after-free is so sneaky.

With 4-byte ints: int *a = malloc(10 * sizeof(int)); int *b = calloc(10, sizeof(int));
Which is TRUE?

  • Both blocks are 40 bytes; only the bytes of b's block are guaranteed to be zero. calloc(num, size) allocates num × size = 40 bytes and zeroes them; malloc leaves whatever was there.
  • Both blocks are 40 bytes; the bytes of both blocks are guaranteed to be zero. malloc does not initialize: reading a's block before writing it gives leftover garbage.
  • Both blocks are 40 bytes; only the bytes of a's block are guaranteed to be zero. Swapped: calloc zeroes, malloc doesn't.
  • a's block is 40 bytes and b's is 10 bytes; only b's bytes are guaranteed to be zero. calloc takes a count and a size: 10 × sizeof(int) = 40 bytes, the same as a.

int *t = realloc(p, 100 * sizeof(int)); succeeds. Which is TRUE?

  • t may equal p or be a new address; the old contents are kept, and from now on you use and free only t. Bilal Ch 14 p.15: the pointer returned may be the same as ptr or a new one. If it moved, realloc copied the data and freed the old block.
  • t always equals p, because realloc grows the block in place; the old contents are kept. If something is in the way, realloc allocates a new block, copies, and frees the old one, so t can differ from p.
  • t may equal p or be a new address; the new block starts zeroed, so you copy the old data over yourself. realloc keeps the old contents (it copies them for you if it moves the block).
  • t may equal p or be a new address; the old contents are kept, and you must free both p and t. If it moved, realloc already freed the old block; if not, p and t are the same block. Either way freeing both is a double free: free only t.
Which bug does this program have?
char *read_name(void) {
    char *n = malloc(32);
    strcpy(n, "zafar");
    return n;
}
int main(void) {
    read_name();
    return 0;
}
  • A memory leak: main throws away the returned address, so the 32-byte block becomes unreachable and the program can never free() it. The block outlives read_name (good), but nobody keeps its address, so it can never be freed.
  • A dangling pointer: n is a local, so the 32-byte block it points to is freed when read_name returns. Only the pointer variable n (on the stack) dies on return. The heap block lives until free(); returning n is fine.
  • A double free: the 32-byte block is freed once when read_name returns and again when main exits. There is no free() at all. Returning from a function never frees heap memory, so this is a leak.
  • A use-after-free: main uses the 32-byte block after read_name's stack frame has been freed. main never uses the block, and a heap block isn't part of any stack frame. The bug is a leak.

Which definition of a dangling pointer is TRUE?

  • A pointer that still holds the address of memory that has already been freed. free() leaves the address in the pointer; using it afterwards is use-after-free (undefined behaviour).
  • A pointer that was set to NULL right after the memory it pointed to was freed. Setting it to NULL is the fix: a NULL pointer no longer points at freed memory.
  • A heap block that is still allocated, but that no pointer refers to any more. That's a leaked (unreachable) block: memory with no pointer, the opposite of a pointer with no memory.
  • A pointer that was declared but never given a valid address to point to. That's forgetting to allocate (an uninitialized pointer), which usually segfaults straight away.
Which bug does this code have?
int *a = malloc(4 * sizeof(int));
int *b = a + 1;
free(a);
b[0] = 9;
  • Use-after-free: b points into the block that free(a) released, so b[0] = 9 writes to freed memory. a and b point into the same block. Freeing it through a makes b dangle too.
  • Memory leak: b still points into the block, so free(a) can't release it and it is never freed. free(a) releases the whole block no matter how many other pointers point into it. Nothing leaks; the bug is the later write through b.
  • Buffer overflow: b[0] lies past the end of the 4-int block, so the write lands outside it. b[0] is a[1], inside the 16-byte block. The problem is that the block was already freed.
  • No bug: only a was freed, so writing through b is still safe. Freeing releases the block, not a name. Every pointer into it, including b, now dangles.

char *buf = malloc(64); strcpy(buf, "os"); free(buf); free(buf); Which is TRUE?

  • It compiles; it's a run-time error that glibc's allocator usually catches, using its block metadata. gcc -Wall may print a warning, but it still builds. glibc's metadata shows the block is already free, so it usually aborts; it isn't guaranteed (undefined behaviour).
  • It usually fails to compile, because the compiler tracks which pointers have already been freed. It can't reject it: buf is a valid char *, so two free(buf) calls are legal C. It's a run-time error.
  • It compiles, and C guarantees the second free() is simply ignored, so it is harmless. It's undefined behaviour: often an abort, sometimes silent heap corruption. Only free(NULL) is guaranteed to do nothing.
  • It compiles; it's a run-time error that the OS kernel usually catches, because free() is a system call. free() is a library call. The allocator (glibc) notices, not the kernel.

memory_leak.c's main is changed to call leaky_function() three times instead of once (4-byte ints). What does valgrind report as definitely lost?

  • 640 bytes in 4 blocks: 40 from arr plus 3 × 200 from the three calls. Each call mallocs a fresh 50 × 4 = 200-byte block and loses it; arr is 10 × 4 = 40.
  • 240 bytes in 2 blocks: 40 from arr plus 200 from the calls, reused each time. Each call runs malloc again and gets a new block; nothing was freed, so nothing can be reused.
  • 600 bytes in 3 blocks: 3 × 200 from the three calls; arr is freed at exit. The OS reclaims memory at exit, but valgrind still counts arr as lost: there's no free() for it.
  • 160 bytes in 4 blocks: 10 from arr plus 3 × 50 from the three calls. Those are int counts. Valgrind reports bytes: × 4 each.

Where exactly does double_free.c stop?

  • Inside free(p) on line 18, so line 19 never prints. The second free finds the block already marked free in glibc's metadata and aborts.
  • Inside free(p) on line 14, so line 15 never prints. The first free is perfectly legal. It's the second one, line 18, that aborts.
  • Inside printf on line 19, after "Freed p twice" prints. The abort happens in line 18, before line 19 can run.
  • At compile time, on line 18, so the program never runs at all. It builds: p is a valid int * (gcc -Wall at most warns). It's a run-time error.

Which is TRUE about line 17 of use_after_free.c, *p = 99;?

  • It compiles and is undefined behaviour; it may corrupt the allocator, and on one run line 19 still printed 99. free() didn't unmap the block or change p, so the write lands in freed heap memory.
  • It fails to compile, because the compiler sees that p was already passed to free(). It's not a compile error. A recent gcc with -Wall may warn (-Wuse-after-free), but it still builds. This is a run-time bug.
  • It compiles and is guaranteed to crash with a segmentation fault on that line. The block is usually still mapped, so there's no guaranteed fault. That's what makes it sneaky.
  • It compiles and writes to address 0, because free(p) set p to NULL. free() can't change p (it gets a copy). p still holds the old heap address.

Which statement about malloc(), free() and the OS is TRUE?

  • malloc() and free() are C library calls; when the heap runs out, the library asks the OS for more using brk/sbrk or mmap. The library manages space inside the heap and only makes a system call when it needs more (Bilal Ch 14 pp.16–17).
  • malloc() and free() are system calls; every call to malloc() traps into the kernel to get memory. They are library calls. Most mallocs never enter the kernel.
  • malloc() and free() are C library calls; every call to free() hands the block straight back to the OS with sbrk. free() normally returns the block to the library's free list for the next malloc, not to the OS.
  • malloc() and free() are C library calls; for small blocks programmers should call brk/sbrk directly, which is faster. Programmers should never call brk/sbrk directly; leave them to malloc.

Which statement about brk / sbrk is TRUE?

  • They move the program break, the address where the heap ends; moving the break up grows the heap. brk(addr) sets the break, sbrk(increment) moves it. The heap grows toward higher addresses, so the break moves up.
  • They move the program break, the address where the stack ends; moving the break down grows the stack. The break marks the end of the heap. The stack grows automatically as functions are called.
  • They move the program break, the address where the heap ends; moving the break down grows the heap. The heap grows toward higher addresses, so the break moves up.
  • They create a new anonymous region somewhere else in the address space, which is how large requests are served. That's mmap. brk/sbrk move the end of the existing heap.

In my_free, what does line 76, (MemBlock *)ptr - 1, compute?

  • The address 24 bytes before ptr, where my_malloc put the block's header. Subtracting 1 from a MemBlock * steps back one whole header (sizeof(MemBlock) = 24).
  • The address 1 byte before ptr, where my_malloc put the block's header. Pointer arithmetic scales by the type: −1 on a MemBlock * is −24 bytes, not −1.
  • The address 24 bytes after ptr, where my_malloc put the block's header. The header sits in front of the data, so you step back.
  • The address 8 bytes before ptr, where my_malloc put the block's size field. It steps back the whole 24-byte header, and the header starts with size, not ends with it.

On an empty list, my_malloc(256) calls request_space(NULL, 256) with a 4096-byte page. Which is TRUE?

  • It mmaps 4096 bytes and writes size = 4072 in the header. 24 + 256 = 280 rounds up to one page; the header's own 24 bytes aren't usable, so size = 4096 − 24.
  • It mmaps 4096 bytes and writes size = 4096 in the header. Line 26 subtracts the header: size = total − HDR = 4072.
  • It mmaps 280 bytes and writes size = 256 in the header. Line 21 rounds up to a whole page: mmap works in pages.
  • It mmaps 8192 bytes and writes size = 8168 in the header. 280 bytes fit in one page. Two pages are only needed above 4096 − 24 = 4072.

Which is TRUE about how my_malloc.c talks to the OS?

  • Only request_space makes a system call (mmap); my_free just sets is_free = 1 and never calls munmap. Same as the real malloc for small blocks: freed memory goes back to the library's list, not to the OS.
  • Only request_space makes a system call (mmap); my_free calls munmap so the OS gets the block back. There's no munmap in my_free (lines 74–83). The block stays mapped for reuse.
  • Every my_malloc call makes a system call (mmap); my_free just sets is_free = 1 and never calls munmap. my_malloc first searches the list (line 60) and only mmaps if nothing free fits.
  • Only request_space makes a system call (sbrk); my_free just sets is_free = 1 and never calls munmap. Line 23 uses mmap, a separate anonymous region, not sbrk.

Lesson 12 · Base and bounds: moving a program without it noticing open lesson ↗

Memory virtualization aims for efficiency and control, as LDE did for the CPU. Which is TRUE?

  • For efficiency, the hardware translates each access; for control, the OS sets up the translation and steps in when something goes wrong. Hardware is fast enough to run on every access; the OS manages it (sets registers, handles faults) without running on each access.
  • For efficiency, the OS translates each access; for control, the hardware sets up the translation and steps in when something goes wrong. Swapped. The hardware translates each access (fast); the OS sets things up and handles faults.
  • For efficiency, the hardware translates each access; for control, the OS checks every access and steps in when something goes wrong. The OS can't run on every access (that would kill efficiency). The hardware does the check too; the OS steps in only on a fault.
  • For efficiency, the hardware translates only loads and stores; for control, the OS sets up the translation and steps in when something goes wrong. Instruction fetches use virtual addresses too: the hardware translates every fetch, load and store.

OSTEP calls address translation an example of interposition. Which is TRUE?

  • The hardware sits between the process and memory and turns each virtual address into a physical one, without the process noticing. OSTEP's tip: the hardware interposes on each memory access. Its usual benefit is transparency: the client needs no changes.
