  • The hardware sits between the process and memory and turns each physical address into a virtual one, without the process noticing. Reversed. The process issues virtual addresses; the hardware turns them into physical ones.
  • The OS sits between the process and memory and turns each virtual address into a physical one, without the process noticing. Wrong actor. Running OS code on every access would be far too slow; the hardware interposes.
  • The hardware sits between the process and memory and turns each virtual address into a physical one, after the process asks with a system call. No request is needed: interposition is transparent. The process just uses its addresses and never notices.

Which list of the first base-and-bounds version's simplifying assumptions is TRUE? Each address space is …

  • … placed contiguously in physical memory, smaller than physical memory, and exactly the same size as every other. These are the three assumptions in OSTEP §15.1 and Dr. Bilal's slides.
  • … placed contiguously in physical memory, larger than physical memory, and exactly the same size as every other. Reversed. It is assumed to be smaller than (less than the size of) physical memory.
  • … placed as separate code, heap and stack pieces in physical memory, smaller than physical memory, and exactly the same size as every other. Splitting into pieces is segmentation, which relaxes this assumption. Here each address space is contiguous (one piece).
  • … placed contiguously in physical memory, smaller than physical memory, and sized to fit its own program. The third assumption is that every address space is exactly the same size.

Every address space is 16 KB and physical memory is 64 KB. Which situation breaks one of the three simplifying assumptions?

  • A's code and heap occupy 16–28 KB and its stack 44–48 KB, with B occupying 28–44 KB. A's address space is split into two pieces with B in between, so it is no longer contiguous: assumption 1 is broken (this is what segmentation allows).
  • A occupies 32–48 KB, and 10 KB of that, between its heap and its stack, is unused. Still one contiguous 16 KB piece, smaller than memory. The unused gap is wasted (internal fragmentation) but breaks no assumption.
  • A occupies 16–32 KB and B occupies 48–64 KB, with 32–48 KB free. Each is one contiguous 16 KB piece, smaller than 64 KB. A free gap between processes breaks no assumption.
  • A occupies 16–32 KB, and while it is not running the OS moves it to 48–64 KB. Relocation just changes the base; A is still one contiguous 16 KB piece. This breaks no assumption.

The three instructions of x = x + 3 (a load at 128, an add at 132, a store at 135; x is at 15 KB) run once. Which is TRUE?

  • They make five memory accesses (three instruction fetches, one load, one store), and every one of them is translated. Fetch 128, load 15 KB, fetch 132, fetch 135, store 15 KB. Instruction fetches use virtual addresses too.
  • They make three memory accesses, one per instruction, and every one of them is translated. Each instruction is fetched from memory, and the load and store also touch data: five accesses.
  • They make six memory accesses (three instruction fetches and one data access each), and every one of them is translated. The add works only on a register (eax), so it has no data access: five in total.
  • They make five memory accesses, but only the load and the store are translated; instruction fetches use physical addresses. The PC holds a virtual address too, so every fetch is translated as well.

Base = 36 KB, bounds = 6 KB (bounds = size). Which translation of virtual address 2,500 is TRUE?

  • 2,500 < 6,144, so it is legal and PA = 36,864 + 2,500 = 39,364. Check first (VA < bounds = 6 × 1024), then add base = 36 × 1024 = 36,864.
  • 2,500 < 6,144, so it is legal and PA = 36,864 − 2,500 = 34,364. You add the base: PA = VA + base = 39,364.
  • 2,500 < 6,144, so it is legal and PA = 6,144 + 2,500 = 8,644. Add the base (36,864), not the bounds. Bounds is only for the check.
  • 2,500 < 6,000, so it is legal and PA = 36,000 + 2,500 = 38,500. KB means 1024: base = 36,864 and bounds = 6,144, so PA = 39,364.

Base = 36 KB, bounds = 6 KB (bounds = size). Which translation of virtual address 6,144 is TRUE?

  • 6,144 is not < 6,144, so the hardware raises an out-of-bounds exception. Valid VAs are 0 … bounds − 1 = 0 … 6,143. VA = bounds is the first byte past the process.
  • 6,144 ≤ 6,144, so it is legal and PA = 36,864 + 6,144 = 43,008. The check is strict: VA < bounds. VA = bounds is already out of bounds.
  • 6,144 < 43,008 (base + bounds), so it is legal and PA = 36,864 + 6,144 = 43,008. Here bounds is a size, so compare the VA with 6,144, not with base + bounds.
  • 6,144 is not < 6,144, so the hardware clamps it to the last legal byte, PA = 43,007. Nothing is clamped: the hardware raises an exception and the OS takes over (usually killing the process).

In the size convention (Dr. Bilal's formula slide), which statement about the bounds register is TRUE?

  • It holds the size of the address space, and the hardware checks 0 ≤ VA < bounds before adding base. Bounds is for protection: check the virtual address first, then relocate with base.
  • It holds the size of the address space, and the hardware checks 0 ≤ PA < bounds after adding base. With bounds = size, the check uses the virtual address, before adding base. (Checking the PA is the end-address convention.)
  • It holds where the process starts in physical memory, and the hardware checks 0 ≤ VA < bounds before adding base. The physical start is the base register. Bounds holds the size.
  • It holds the size of the address space, and the hardware relocates with it: PA = VA + bounds. Relocation uses base: PA = VA + base. Bounds is only for the protection check.

This machine stores the physical end address in the bounds register. Base = 50 KB, bounds = 60 KB. Which translation of virtual address 10,000 is TRUE?

  • PA = 51,200 + 10,000 = 61,200, and 61,200 < 61,440, so it is legal. End-address convention: add base first, then check the PA against bounds (60 × 1024 = 61,440).
  • PA = 50,000 + 10,000 = 60,000, and 60,000 is not < 60,000, so it faults. KB means 1024: base = 51,200 and bounds = 61,440, so PA = 61,200 is legal.
  • PA = 51,200 + 10,000 = 61,200, and 61,200 is not < 10,240, so it faults. 10,240 is the size. In this convention the PA is compared with the end address, 61,440.

What does test_translation(1, 500, 67) print in mmu_simple.c, and why?

  • [FAULT], because line 40 tests virtual_address >= bounds and 500 >= 500. Bounds = size = 500, so the legal VAs are 0 … 499.
  • [OK] with PA 1500, because line 40 tests virtual_address > bounds and 500 > 500 is false. The code uses >=, not >. VA = bounds is out of bounds.
  • [FAULT], because line 40 tests base + virtual_address >= bounds and 1500 >= 500. Line 40 compares the virtual address with bounds; base is added later, on line 42.
  • [OK] with PA 1500, because line 40 only rejects negative virtual addresses. Line 40 has two tests: VA < 0 or VA >= bounds.

In translate(), which pairing of lines and jobs is TRUE?

  • Line 40 does protection (the bounds check) and line 42 does relocation (adding base). Check first, then add: the same order as the hardware in the size convention.
  • Line 40 does relocation (adding base) and line 42 does protection (the bounds check). Swapped: line 40 is the if against bounds; line 42 adds base.
  • Line 42 does protection (the bounds check) and line 40 does nothing once bounds = size. Line 40 is the size-convention bounds check; line 42 has no check at all.
  • Line 40 does protection (the bounds check) and line 42 does relocation (adding bounds). Relocation adds the base: base + virtual_address.

mmu_virus.c with CHECK_BOUNDS 0: what does attack("x", 2, SEG_HEAP, 700) print? (PID 2's heap: base 2000, bounds 600.)

  • ALLOWED -> PA=2700, even though 700 is past the heap's 600 bytes. With the check compiled out, line 55 just computes 2000 + 700.
  • BLOCKED (bounds error), because 700 is past the heap's 600 bytes. With CHECK_BOUNDS 0, lines 49–50 are removed by the preprocessor, so nothing is blocked.
  • ALLOWED -> PA=1300, even though 700 is past the heap's 600 bytes. Only the stack subtracts (line 54). The heap adds: 2000 + 700.
  • ALLOWED -> PA=2600, because offsets past the bounds are clamped to it. Nothing clamps: the raw offset is added, giving 2700.

Why must the instructions that change the base and bounds registers be privileged?

  • A user process could otherwise point base at another process's (or the OS's) memory, so protection would be lost. Only the OS, in kernel mode, may set them. A user-mode attempt raises an exception.
  • A user process could otherwise point base at another process's memory, so the hardware silently ignores such attempts in user mode. The hardware doesn't ignore it: it raises an exception, and the OS usually terminates the process.
  • A user process could otherwise change them so often that translation slows down, so efficiency would be lost. The reason is protection: whoever controls base can reach any physical memory.
  • The OS has to change them on every memory access, and only kernel mode is fast enough for that. The hardware translates every access. The OS sets base/bounds only at a few moments (process start, context switch).

The OS switches the CPU from process A to process B. What does it do with base and bounds?

  • It saves A's base and bounds into A's PCB, then loads B's saved base and bounds into the registers. There is only one pair of registers per CPU, so each process's values live in its PCB while it isn't running.
  • Nothing: every process has its own base and bounds registers in the MMU, so they never need changing. There is only one pair per CPU, so the OS must save A's and restore B's.
  • It saves A's base and bounds into A's PCB, then copies B's address space into A's old physical slot. No copying is needed: B's memory stays where it is, and the OS just loads B's base and bounds.
  • It saves A's base and bounds into A's PCB, then sets base = 0 and bounds = all of RAM while B runs. That would let B reach everyone's memory. The OS loads B's own saved base and bounds.

A running process accesses a virtual address beyond its bounds. Which is TRUE?

  • The hardware raises an exception, switches to kernel mode and runs the OS's handler, which usually terminates the process. The handler was registered in the trap table at boot. The usual reaction is to kill the offending process and reclaim its memory.
  • The hardware raises an exception, switches to kernel mode and runs the OS's handler, which usually raises bounds so the access succeeds. Base and bounds has no "grow on demand". The usual reaction is to terminate the process.
  • The OS checks each address in software, notices the bad one and terminates the process before the access happens. The hardware does the check on every access. The OS only runs once the exception fires.
  • The hardware raises an exception, stays in user mode and jumps to the process's own error-handling code. It switches to kernel mode and runs the OS's handler from the trap table.

Process P is not running. The OS wants to move it from physical 16 KB to physical 64 KB. Which is TRUE?

  • The OS copies P's address space to 64 KB and updates the saved base in P's PCB to 64 KB; P never notices. When P next runs, the new base is loaded and every virtual address still works (OSTEP §15.5).
  • The OS copies P's address space to 64 KB and rewrites every address in P's code to add 48 KB. Rewriting addresses is static relocation. With base and bounds only the saved base changes.
  • The OS copies P's address space to 64 KB and updates the saved bounds in P's PCB to 64 KB. The size hasn't changed, so bounds stays the same. The base becomes 64 KB.
  • The OS updates the saved base in P's PCB to 64 KB; the hardware copies the data over on P's next access. The hardware never copies memory. The OS must copy the address space itself.

Process A is running normally under base and bounds (no system calls, timer interrupts or faults). Which is TRUE?

  • The OS is not involved: the hardware translates and checks every access itself, and the OS steps in only on a trap or interrupt. This is limited direct execution for memory: the OS sets things up, then gets out of the way.
  • The OS translates each address in software, and the hardware only raises an exception if bounds is exceeded. Translation is done by hardware on every access; doing it in software would be far too slow.
  • The hardware adds base to each address, and the OS checks each result against bounds in software. The bounds check is hardware too. The OS isn't involved on each access, only on exceptions.
  • The OS is not involved, but it reloads base and bounds from A's PCB after every instruction. Base and bounds are loaded when A is scheduled (at a context switch), not after every instruction.

Every process gets a fixed 16 KB slot. One process uses 3 KB of code, 2 KB of heap and 1 KB of stack. Which is TRUE?

  • 10 KB of the slot is wasted, inside the allocated block; this is internal fragmentation. Used = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 KB, so 16 − 6 = 10 KB of free gap still takes physical memory.
  • 10 KB of the slot is wasted, inside the allocated block; this is external fragmentation. Waste inside an allocated block is internal. External is holes between blocks (segmentation).
  • 6 KB of the slot is wasted, inside the allocated block; this is internal fragmentation. 6 KB is what's used. The waste is 16 − 6 = 10 KB.
  • Nothing is wasted, because the free gap between heap and stack takes no physical memory. Base and bounds reserves the whole slot, gap included. Avoiding that is what segmentation is for.

Lesson 13 · Segmentation: a base and bounds for every piece open lesson ↗

Code: virtual 0–4 KB, physical base 20 KB, size 2 KB. Heap: virtual 4–8 KB, physical base 46 KB, size 3 KB, grows up. Which translation of heap address VA 5,000 is TRUE?

  • Offset = 5,000 − 4,096 = 904 < 3,072, so PA = 47,104 + 904 = 48,008. Offset is measured from the heap's virtual start (4 KB). Check against the heap's size, then add the heap's base (46 × 1024).
  • Offset = 5,000 < 8,192, so PA = 47,104 + 5,000 = 52,104. Adding base to the whole VA is the #1 slip. Subtract the heap's virtual start first: offset = 904.
  • Offset = 5,000 − 4,096 = 904 < 3,072, so PA = 20,480 + 904 = 21,384. 20 KB is the code segment's base. VA 5,000 is in the heap, so add the heap's base, 47,104.
  • Offset = 5,000 − 4,096 = 904 < 3,072, so PA = 47,104 − 904 = 46,200. The heap grows up, so you add the offset: 47,104 + 904 = 48,008.

14-bit virtual addresses; the top 2 bits select the segment: 00 code, 01 heap, 10 unused, 11 stack. Which statement is TRUE?

  • Heap addresses are 4,096–8,191 and stack addresses are 12,288–16,383. Each selector value owns a 4 KB (4,096-byte) slice: 01 → 4 KB–8 KB, 11 → 12 KB–16 KB.
  • Heap addresses are 4,096–8,191 and stack addresses are 8,192–12,287. 8 KB–12 KB is selector 10, unused in this table. Stack is 11: 12,288–16,383.
  • Heap addresses are 4,000–7,999 and stack addresses are 12,000–15,999. KB means 1024: heap 4,096–8,191, stack 12,288–16,383.
  • Heap addresses are 0–4,095 and stack addresses are 12,288–16,383. 0–4,095 is selector 00, the code. The heap (01) is 4,096–8,191.

A 32-bit virtual address uses its top 4 bits as the segment selector. Which is TRUE?

  • There can be 16 segments, each at most 228 bytes = 256 MB. Segments = 2s = 24 = 16. Offset bits n = 32 − 4 = 28, so max size = 228 = 28 MB = 256 MB.
  • There can be 4 segments, each at most 228 bytes = 256 MB. 4 is the number of selector bits. Segments = 24 = 16.
  • There can be 16 segments, each at most 228 bytes = 512 MB. 228 = 28 × 220 = 256 MB. (512 MB is 229.)
  • There can be 16 segments, each at most 232 bytes = 4 GB. Only the 28 offset bits address bytes inside a segment: max size = 228 = 256 MB.

14-bit virtual addresses with a 2-bit segment selector at the top. Which set of constants is TRUE?

  • SEG_MASK = 0x3000, SEG_SHIFT = 12, OFFSET_MASK = 0xFFF. SEG_MASK = 11 0000 0000 0000 (bits 13–12); shift by the 12 offset bits; OFFSET_MASK = 12 ones.
  • SEG_MASK = 0x3000, SEG_SHIFT = 2, OFFSET_MASK = 0xFFF. Shift by the number of offset bits (12), not selector bits, to bring bits 13–12 down to the bottom.
  • SEG_MASK = 0xC000, SEG_SHIFT = 12, OFFSET_MASK = 0xFFF. 0xC000 is the top 2 bits of a 16-bit address. For 14 bits the top two are bits 13–12: 0x3000.
  • SEG_MASK = 0x3000, SEG_SHIFT = 12, OFFSET_MASK = 0x3FFF. 0x3FFF is all 14 bits. The offset is only the low 12 bits: 0xFFF.

14-bit VA 7,000 with SEG_MASK = 0x3000, SEG_SHIFT = 12, OFFSET_MASK = 0xFFF. Which is TRUE?

  • VA & SEG_MASK = 4,096; shifting right by 12 gives segment 1; VA & OFFSET_MASK = 2,904. 7,000 = 01 1011 0101 1000. Masking keeps 01 in bits 13–12 (= 4,096); the shift brings it down to 1. Offset = 7,000 − 4,096.
  • VA & SEG_MASK = 1, which is already the segment number; VA & OFFSET_MASK = 2,904. Masking only zeroes the other bits; the selector stays in its high position, so the result is 4,096. The shift turns it into 1.
  • VA & SEG_MASK = 4,096; shifting right by 12 gives segment 1; VA & OFFSET_MASK = 7,000. OFFSET_MASK strips the selector bits: 7,000 & 0xFFF = 2,904.

14-bit VA, top 2 bits select the segment, max segment size 4 KB. Heap: selector 01, virtual 4–8 KB, base 30 KB, size 2 KB, grows up. Which translation of VA 6,300 is TRUE?

  • Offset = 6,300 − 4,096 = 2,204, which is not < 2,048 (the heap's size), so it is a segmentation fault. The address is inside the heap's 4 KB slot but past its current 2 KB size.
  • Offset = 6,300 − 4,096 = 2,204 < 4,096 (the max segment size), so PA = 30,720 + 2,204 = 32,924. Check against the segment's actual size (2,048), not the 4 KB slot. 2,204 ≥ 2,048 → fault.
  • The VA lies in the heap's range 4–8 KB, so it is legal and PA = 30,720 + 6,300 = 37,020. Strip the selector bits first: offset = 2,204, which is past the 2 KB size → fault.
  • Offset = 6,300 − 4,096 = 2,204, which is not < 2,048, so the hardware grows the heap and PA = 32,924. The hardware never grows a segment: it faults. The heap grows only when malloc asks the OS (sbrk).

14-bit VA, top 2 bits select the segment (11 = stack), 12-bit offset, so the max segment size is 4,096. Stack: virtual 12–16 KB, physical base 36 KB, size 3 KB, grows down. Which translation of VA 14,500 is TRUE?

  • Offset 2,212; negative offset 2,212 − 4,096 = −1,884; |−1,884| ≤ 3,072, so PA = 36,864 − 1,884 = 34,980. Offset = 14,500 − 12,288. Subtract the max segment size, check against the actual size, then PA = base + negative offset.
  • Offset 2,212; 2,212 < 3,072 so it is in bounds, and PA = 36,864 + 2,212 = 39,076. The stack grows down: use the negative offset 2,212 − 4,096 = −1,884, giving 34,980.
  • Offset 2,212; negative offset 2,212 − 3,072 = −860; |−860| ≤ 3,072, so PA = 36,864 − 860 = 36,004. Subtract the max segment size (4,096), not the stack's actual size: −1,884 → 34,980.
  • Offset 2,212; the stack grows down, so PA = 36,864 − 2,212 = 34,652. The raw offset counts up from the bottom of the 4 KB slot. Convert it first: 2,212 − 4,096 = −1,884 → 34,980.

14-bit VA, top 2 bits select the segment (11 = stack), 12-bit offset, so the max segment size is 4,096. Stack: virtual 12–16 KB, physical base 36 KB, size 3 KB, grows down. Which translation of VA 12,900 is TRUE?

  • Offset 612; negative offset 612 − 4,096 = −3,484; |−3,484| > 3,072, so it is a segmentation fault. Offset = 12,900 − 12,288. The address is 3,484 below the top, but the stack only extends 3,072 below base.
  • Offset 612; negative offset 612 − 4,096 = −3,484, so PA = 36,864 − 3,484 = 33,380. You skipped the bounds check: |−3,484| > 3,072 (the stack's size), so it faults.
  • Offset 612; 612 < 3,072 so it is in bounds, and PA = 36,864 + 612 = 37,476. For a stack, check the negative offset: |612 − 4,096| = 3,484 > 3,072 → fault.
  • Offset 612; negative offset 612 − 3,072 = −2,460; |−2,460| ≤ 3,072, so PA = 36,864 − 2,460 = 34,404. Subtract the max segment size (4,096): −3,484, which is out of bounds → fault.

A stack segment has base B and size S, and grows down (negative direction). Which statement is TRUE?

  • B is the top (high end) of the stack's physical region; its valid bytes run from B − S up to B − 1. PA = B + negative offset, with −S ≤ negative offset ≤ −1. The highest virtual address (offset = max segment size − 1, negative offset −1) lands at B − 1.
  • B is the bottom (low end) of the stack's physical region; its valid bytes run from B up to B + S − 1. That's a segment that grows up (code, heap). For the stack, base is the top.
  • B is the top (high end) of the stack's physical region; its valid bytes run from B up to B + S − 1. If B is the top, the bytes lie below it: B − S … B − 1.
  • B is the top (high end) of the stack's physical region; its valid bytes run from B − 4 KB (the max segment size) up to B − 1. Only the stack's actual size S is backed by memory: B − S … B − 1. The 4 KB slot is just the virtual range.

What does segmented_translate(1, SEG_STACK, 120, &pa) do? (PID 1's stack: base 4000, bounds 500.)

  • Returns SUCCESS with PA = 3880, because line 99 computes 4000 − 120. 120 < 500 passes line 94, and the stack subtracts the offset from its base.
  • Returns SUCCESS with PA = 4120, because line 101 computes 4000 + 120. Line 98 sends the stack to line 99, which subtracts. Only the other segments add.
  • Returns SUCCESS with PA = 24, because it computes 4000 + (120 − 4096). That's the exam formula applied to the wrong kind of offset. The lab code just does base − offset.
  • Returns ERROR_BOUNDS, because a stack offset must be negative to pass line 94. Line 94 rejects offsets below 0. The lab's stack offsets are positive distances down from base.

Stack base B, size S. Which comparison of the two conventions is TRUE?

  • Lab offset 0 maps to PA = B; in the exam convention the highest stack VA maps to PA = B − 1. Lab: B − 0. Exam: neg = (max − 1) − max = −1, so B − 1.
  • Lab offset 0 maps to PA = B; in the exam convention the highest stack VA also maps to PA = B. In the exam convention neg is at most −1, so PA never reaches B: the top byte is B − 1.
  • Lab offset 0 maps to PA = B − 1; in the exam convention the highest stack VA maps to PA = B − 1. Line 99 with offset 0 gives B − 0 = B.
  • Lab offset 0 maps to PA = B; in the exam convention the highest stack VA maps to PA = B − S. B − S is the lowest stack byte (neg = −S). The highest VA gives neg = −1.

Why does mmu_segmented.c never use SEG_MASK or SEG_SHIFT?

  • Its caller passes the segment number and the offset as two separate arguments, so there are no selector bits to extract. An exam question gives one raw VA instead; then you mask and shift to split it.
  • Its caller passes one raw virtual address, and line 93 extracts the segment with SEG_MASK. Line 93 just copies p->segments[segment]; the segment arrives ready-made as an argument.
  • It uses the implicit approach, so the segment is chosen by how the address was formed. Nothing is inferred: the segment is passed explicitly as the second argument.
  • Its caller passes the segment number and offset separately, so the stack needs the max segment size instead. The lab's stack uses base − offset; max segment size appears only in the exam's raw-VA method.

In the implicit approach, how does the hardware decide which segment an address is in?

  • From how the address was formed: from the program counter → code; based on the stack or base pointer → stack; otherwise → heap. OSTEP §16.2: no selector bits, so the hardware looks at where the address came from.
  • From the top bits of the virtual address: 00 → code, 01 → heap, 11 → stack. Using the top bits is the explicit approach. Implicit uses how the address was formed.
  • From how the address was formed: from the program counter → code; based on the stack or base pointer → heap; otherwise → stack. Addresses based on the stack or base pointer belong to the stack; everything else is the heap.

Which statement about code sharing with segmentation is TRUE?

  • Code is marked read-execute, so several processes can safely share one physical copy; a write to it raises an exception. Per-segment protection bits make sharing safe, and each process still thinks the code is its own private memory.
  • Code is marked read-write, so several processes can share one physical copy and see each other's changes. Shared code is marked read-execute (no write), so no process can change the shared copy.
  • Code is marked read-execute, so several processes can safely share one physical copy; a write to it is silently ignored. The hardware checks the protection bits and raises an exception on a write.
  • Code is marked read-execute, so several processes can safely share one physical copy, though each can tell it is shared. Sharing stays transparent: each process still thinks the code is its own private memory.

Which statement about coarse-grained vs fine-grained segmentation is TRUE?

  • Coarse-grained has a few large segments kept in MMU registers; fine-grained has many small segments, kept in a segment table in memory. Code/heap/stack fit in a few base-bounds register pairs. Thousands of segments need a segment table in memory (with hardware support).
  • Coarse-grained has many small segments kept in MMU registers; fine-grained has a few large segments, kept in a segment table in memory. Sizes swapped. Coarse = a few large chunks (code, heap, stack); fine = many small ones.
  • Coarse-grained has a few large segments kept in a segment table in memory; fine-grained has many small segments, kept in MMU registers. Locations swapped. A few segments fit in MMU registers; thousands of segments don't, so fine-grained needs a table in memory.
  • Coarse-grained has a few large segments kept in MMU registers; fine-grained has many small segments, needing no extra hardware support. Supporting many segments needs further hardware support: a segment table in memory that the hardware uses.

OSTEP mentions early machines like the Burroughs B5000, which supported thousands of segments. Which is TRUE?

  • That is fine-grained segmentation: the compiler chops code and data into many small segments, tracked in a segment table in memory. OSTEP 16.5: early systems such as the Burroughs B5000 used many small segments, which need a segment table in memory.
  • That is coarse-grained segmentation: the compiler chops code and data into many small segments, tracked in a segment table in memory. Many small segments is fine-grained. Coarse-grained means a few large ones (code, heap, stack).
  • That is fine-grained segmentation: the compiler chops code and data into many small segments, tracked in one register pair each. There aren't thousands of register pairs in the MMU; the segment info lives in a segment table in memory.
  • That is fine-grained segmentation: the OS chops each program into many small segments as it loads it, tracked in a segment table in memory. Wrong actor. OSTEP: the B5000 expected the compiler to chop code and data into segments, which the OS and hardware then support.

Free physical memory consists of holes of 5 KB, 7 KB and 6 KB between segments. A new 10 KB segment is requested. Which is TRUE?

  • No hole can hold it as memory stands: 18 KB is free in total, but no single hole is 10 KB. This is external fragmentation. A segment must be contiguous. Holes between variable-sized segments = external fragmentation.
  • No hole can hold it as memory stands: 18 KB is free in total, but no single hole is 10 KB. This is internal fragmentation. Waste between allocated blocks is external. Internal is waste inside a block (base and bounds).
  • It can be placed as memory stands: 18 KB is free in total, and the segment is split across the holes. A segment is one contiguous range with a single base, so it can't be split.
  • No hole can hold it as memory stands: 18 KB is free in total, but no single hole is 10 KB. Using best-fit would remove this problem completely. Free-list algorithms only minimise external fragmentation. Only compaction merges the holes, at a high cost.
